articles.title: ABB and Oreve plan 12 new electric truck charging sites in France
articles.summary: ABB E-mobility and French charging operator Oreve have expanded their partnership to develop 12 new high-power charging sites along major freight corridors in France. The expansion will add approximately 100 charging points, with a combined installed capacity of around 18 MW once the new sites are fully deployed by...
articles.body: ABB E-mobility and French charging operator Oreve have expanded their partnership to develop 12 new high-power charging sites along major freight corridors in France. The expansion will add approximately 100 charging points, with a combined installed capacity of around 18 MW once the new sites are fully deployed by the end of 2028. The project aims to support the growing use of electric trucks in road freight transport. It will also provide additional charging capacity for passenger vehicles. Under the agreement, ABB E-mobility will supply the charging equipment, cloud-based management technology and technical support services. The two companies have worked together for three years and currently operate six charging sites through their partnership. These include locations in Bourg-de-Péage, Vénissieux and Pardies. New charging infrastructure to support freight transport The planned sites will use ABB E-mobility’s A400 and M-Series charging systems. Initially, the new locations will feature A400 chargers, which can distribute up to 400 kW of power between two charging points. From early 2027, the rollout will also include the M-Series modular charging system. This technology allows operators to increase charging capacity as demand grows, without replacing the entire underlying infrastructure. According to ABB E-mobility, the system can support charging hubs with capacities of up to 1.2 MW. In addition, the M-Series supports both Combined Charging System (CCS) and Megawatt Charging System (MCS) technology. The first MCS-capable installation under the expanded partnership is planned for 2027. France prepares to expand truck charging network The investment comes as France develops its national charging infrastructure for heavy-duty vehicles. The country’s road-network charging plan envisages approximately 8,000 truck charging points across around 560 motorway service and rest areas by 2035. These facilities are expected to provide approximately 1.6 GW of dedicated charging capacity along major freight routes. Nicolas Dourassoff, CEO of Oreve, said the company intends to expand its charging infrastructure in line with developments in electric truck technology. Meanwhile, Bruno Bourguet, President EMEA at ABB E-mobility, highlighted the importance of scalable charging systems that can accommodate growing demand from freight operators. The expanded partnership builds on the companies’ existing network in France. However, the 12 additional sites remain under development, with full deployment targeted for the end of 2028.

Join the leading maritime news network Improving vessel energy efficiency is an important part of the maritime industry’s efforts to reduce fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. While hull performance often receives significant attention, the condition of a vessel’s propeller also plays an important role in maintaining propulsion efficiency throughout its operating cycle. Propspeed has joined RightShip’s Zero Harm Innovation Partners Program, bringing its expertise in biocide-free, foul-release propeller coatings to a collaborative network focused on advancing safer and more sustainable maritime operations. Through the Program, Propspeed aims to raise awareness of the role propeller surface condition plays in vessel performance and how coating technologies can help shipowners and managers manage efficiency losses associated with biofouling and propeller surface condition. A vessel’s propulsion efficiency depends on several factors, including the condition of its hull and propeller surfaces. Over time, operational wear, marine growth, corrosion, cavitation erosion and mechanical damage can increase surface roughness, affecting the flow of water across propeller blades. As surface roughness increases, more power may be required to maintain vessel speed, contributing to higher fuel consumption, operating costs and associated emissions. Although propellers account for a relatively small proportion of a vessel’s total wetted surface area, fouling on these surfaces can have a disproportionately large effect on propulsion efficiency. The extent of deterioration depends on factors such as vessel operating conditions, trading patterns, ports of call and periods spent idle. Managing propeller surface condition is therefore an important consideration in maintaining vessel performance between scheduled dry dockings. Propspeed has developed a biocide-free coating system specifically designed for propeller surfaces, helping protect propeller efficiency by reducing surface roughness, while also limiting the accumulation of marine growth and its impact on performance. The system consists of two components: an etching primer that bonds to the metal substrate and a silicone-based foul-release topcoat. Together, they create an ultra-smooth, hydrophobic surface that helps reduce propeller surface roughness and makes it more difficult for marine organisms to adhere. Applied during scheduled dry docking, the coating is designed to help preserve propeller surface condition as vessels return to service and throughout their operating cycle. This approach addresses a particular challenge in marine coating applications. Propellers operate in demanding environments, where coatings must withstand mechanical and operational stresses while maintaining adhesion and foul-release properties. By helping reduce surface roughness from day of application and limiting additional roughness caused by biofouling, Propspeed’s technology aims to support more consistent propulsion efficiency between dockings. Maintaining propeller efficiency has implications beyond vessel performance. By reducing the additional power demand associated with increased surface roughness, effective propeller maintenance can contribute to lower fuel consumption and associated greenhouse gas emissions. Propspeed’s approach also considers the environmental implications of biofouling management. Its coating system does not rely on biocides to discourage marine growth. Instead, the silicone-based surface is designed to make it harder for organisms to attach, supporting biofouling management while potentially reducing the risk of transferring invasive aquatic species between marine environments. The foul-release properties may also reduce the need for repeated underwater propeller polishing during a coating’s service life. Where this reduces the frequency of diving interventions, it could help limit associated costs and occupational safety exposure. These potential benefits illustrate how attention to a specific component of vessel performance can contribute to broader operational and sustainability objectives. Actual efficiency improvements and fuel savings will depend on vessel-specific conditions and operating practices. Propspeed’s participation in RightShip’s Zero Harm Innovation Partners Program reflects a shared interest in practical technologies that can contribute to safer and more sustainable maritime operations. Through the Program, Propspeed aims to encourage greater industry awareness of propeller efficiency and its contribution to vessel energy performance. This includes promoting a more considered approach to propeller maintenance alongside other vessel efficiency measures. RightShip’s Zero Harm Innovation Partners Program brings together organisations across the maritime supply chain to encourage the development and adoption of technologies and solutions that support the industry’s journey towards Zero Harm. By fostering knowledge sharing and long-term collaboration, the Program aims to support coordinated progress on safety and sustainability challenges. As part of this network, Propspeed brings a focused approach to managing propeller surface condition and its implications for vessel efficiency. RightShip looks forward to working with Propspeed to encourage knowledge exchange and greater awareness of practical approaches that can support more efficient and environmentally responsible maritime operations. articles.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard is exploring the use of commercial icebreaking vessels to help keep Northeast ports and waterways open this winter, as the service prepares for another season of...

Join the leading maritime news network Coast Guard Cutter Penobscot Bay, a 140-foot bay-class icebreaking tug, breaks ice on the Hudson River in support of Operation Reliable Energy for Northeast Winters (OPRENEW), February 11, 2021. OPRENEW is the Coast Guard's effort to keep waterways clear of ice during the winter months. (U.S. Coast Guard photo illustration by Petty Officer 3rd Class Anthony Pappaly) The U.S. Coast Guard is exploring the use of commercial icebreaking vessels to help keep Northeast ports and waterways open this winter, as the service prepares for another season of potentially disruptive ice conditions. In an October 21 Request for Information (RFI) posted on SAM.gov, the Coast Guard is seeking U.S.-flag, Jones Act-qualified vessels capable of supporting emergency icebreaking operations across New England and southern Connecticut. The goal is to maintain commercial shipping channels, ensure deliveries of critical cargo, and reduce navigational risks during periods of heavy ice. The Coast Guard is looking for vessels capable of operating in ice ranging from 4 to 18 inches thick, with the ability to mobilize to the Northeast by January 2, 2027. Potential operating areas include Boston Harbor, the Cape Cod Canal, Buzzards Bay, Nantucket, Martha’s Vineyard, Narragansett Bay, and Connecticut ports including Bridgeport, Stamford, and New Haven. Under the proposed arrangement, commercial operators would provide the vessels, crews, equipment, and supervision, while the Coast Guard would direct operational priorities. The service anticipates providing 72 hours’ notice before operations, with a minimum seven-day operating window for continuous support. Vessels would be expected to work up to 12 hours per day during daylight hours, with longer operations requiring approval. The Coast Guard is also asking operators to describe their ability to clear shipping channels, maintain navigable tracks, escort vessels carrying critical cargo, and assist communities affected by ice jams or flooding. Only U.S.-flag, coastwise-qualified vessels will be considered. The request follows a difficult 2025–2026 winter that saw severe ice conditions across the Northeast and Great Lakes, forcing the Coast Guard to deploy icebreaking assets to maintain commercial navigation. In January, the Coast Guard launched Operation Reliable Energy for Northeast Winters (RENEW), emphasizing the importance of keeping heating oil and other essential supplies moving through the region’s waterways. At the time, the service acknowledged that some icebreaking assets were undergoing maintenance and upgrades, requiring operational adjustments to concentrate resources where they were most needed. The new commercial vessel initiative also comes as the Coast Guard moves forward with plans to modernize its aging domestic icebreaking fleet. The service is pursuing the acquisition of up to seven Homeland Security Cutter–Light Icebreakers to replace its aging 65-foot icebreaking tugs, which perform critical winter missions throughout the Northeast. The Coast Guard issued a formal solicitation for the new vessels earlier this year, with final proposals due in October. The commercial icebreaking request could provide another option for meeting near-term winter demands while that modernization effort moves forward. For now, the Coast Guard is conducting market research rather than soliciting binding bids. The agency is requesting information on vessel capabilities, previous icebreaking experience, mobilization timelines, operating limitations, and potential contract structures. Operators may also submit preliminary pricing information, including daily rates and mobilization costs. The RFI does not specify how many commercial vessels may ultimately be needed or the potential value of a future contract. Responses are due November 13, 2026, at 5 p.m. Eastern. The Coast Guard emphasized that the notice is for planning purposes only and does not guarantee a future solicitation or contract award. articles.title: Tubarão Gains, Ponta da Madeira Retreats: Brazil’s Iron Ore Freight Outlook
articles.summary: Brazilian iron ore exports have diverged across major loading systems in 2026. Tubarão has recorded stronger China-bound shipments, while Ponta da Madeira (PDM) has declined amid weaker output at Vale’s Northern System. The difference matters for freight, but cargo growth alone does not establish additional spot...
articles.body: Tubarão Gains, Ponta da Madeira Retreats: Brazil’s Iron Ore Freight Outlook in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 05/11/2026 Brazilian iron ore exports have diverged across major loading systems in 2026. Tubarão has recorded stronger China-bound shipments, while Ponta da Madeira (PDM) has declined amid weaker output at Vale’s Northern System. The difference matters for freight, but cargo growth alone does not establish additional spot Capesize demand: vessel size, contractual coverage and the timing of Atlantic ballast arrivals determine how much export activity reaches the C3 market. Brazilian terminals | China-bound export divergence Tubarão’s estimated China-bound shipments increased by 6.59 Mt to 40.07 Mt in January–September 2026, up 20% year on year. Ponta da Madeira moved in the opposite direction, losing 9.90 Mt to 78.80 Mt (−11%). Guaíba recorded a more modest increase of 4% to 24.23 Mt, while the wider Itaguaí area declined 6% to 36.07 Mt. The contrast indicates that Brazil’s China trade is not strengthening evenly across its export corridors. Across all destinations, Tubarão’s iron ore loadings increased by approximately 6.3 Mt (+11%) year on year during January–September 2026, while Ponta da Madeira declined by 10.8 Mt (−9%). Figure 1 highlights the contrasting export performance of Vale’s Southeastern and Northern Systems, with Tubarão recording stronger loading activity amid weaker volumes at Ponta da Madeira. Monthly loadings | Tubarão steadier, PDM recovering from September Figure 2 presents monthly iron ore loadings to all export destinations, with October volumes remaining indicative. Tubarão recorded a rebound in loading activity during 2026, with volumes strengthening from the lower levels seen earlier in the year and remaining firm through the third quarter. September loadings reached approximately 7.4 Mt, with October indications rising slightly to 7.5 Mt. Ponta da Madeira followed a more variable monthly pattern, despite its weaker cumulative export performance year on year. Its October loading indications increased to approximately 15.2 Mt from 13.5 Mt in September (+13%). Ponta da Madeira’s performance also reflects developments within Vale’s Northern System. According to Vale’s third-quarter results, Northern System iron ore production declined by 6.9 Mt year on year to 42.8 Mt, largely reflecting reduced run-of-mine availability at Serra Norte, while stronger Serra Sul output provided a partial offset. Vale nevertheless maintained its full-year production guidance of 335–345 Mt, expecting operational improvements during the final quarter. These developments provide important context for PDM’s export performance, although production volumes and seaborne loadings do not necessarily move in parallel. The improvement in loading activity was also reflected across Brazilian iron ore export ports, where estimated volumes reached 28.4 Mt during 1–25 October, up 5.8% from the corresponding September period but 2.3% below the same period in 2025. The month-on-month increase points to firmer shipment activity, although the year-on-year decline indicates that the recovery remains uneven across Brazil’s export terminals. Port Insights | Tubarão Leads in Conventional Capesize Nominations The 28 October Port Insights data show contrasting iron ore loading programmes at Tubarão and Ponta da Madeira. Tubarão recorded 67 nominated loading calls representing 13.16 Mt, compared with 57 calls and 14.74 Mt at Ponta da Madeira. Conventional Capesizes accounted for 44 calls (7.33 Mt) at Tubarão, compared with 24 calls (4.15 Mt) at PDM. In contrast, PDM’s programme was dominated by 33 VLOC nominations representing 10.59 Mt, against 16 VLOC calls (5.38 Mt) at Tubarão. Despite PDM’s larger nominated cargo volume, Tubarão recorded 20 more conventional Capesize calls, highlighting the different vessel requirements at the two terminals. The November departure schedules reinforce this difference. Tubarão recorded approximately 10.7 Mt of nominated departures, including 38 conventional Capesize calls (6.32 Mt) and 12 VLOC calls (3.96 Mt). At Ponta da Madeira, November nominations reached approximately 11.3 Mt, comprising 25 VLOC calls (7.91 Mt) and 20 conventional Capesize calls (3.40 Mt). The higher VLOC concentration at PDM contrasts with Tubarão’s stronger conventional Capesize representation, an important distinction when assessing potential vessel employment on Brazil’s long-haul iron ore routes. Cargo composition provides further context. At Tubarão, iron ore pellets accounted for 51 nominated calls and approximately 7.78 Mt, or 59% of indicated tonnage. At Ponta da Madeira, iron ore fines dominated the loading programme, with VLOCs representing approximately 72% of nominated cargo tonnage. The contrasting cargo and vessel profiles highlight how differences in export activity between the two ports translate into different fleet requirements. The nominated programmes provide a forward view of potential loading activity, while actual Capesize employment will depend on the execution of scheduled departures and the availability of vessels positioning towards Brazil. Production outlook | Supply constraints Brazil’s iron ore production outlook remains uneven. Vale reported 88.4 Mt in the third quarter, down 6% year on year, with lower ore availability at Serra Norte partly offset by stronger Serra Sul performance. Both operations belong to the Northern System, providing operational context for weaker exports through Ponta da Madeira. Vale nevertheless maintained its annual guidance of 335–345 Mt. The extent to which production translates into export availability will depend on inventories, logistics and the execution of loading programmes. Supply pressure is more evident among smaller producers. CSN Mineração reduced its production-plus-purchases guidance to 39–41 Mt from 45–47 Mt, while several independent miners announced suspensions or output adjustments. These developments coincide with weaker terminal activity: combined September–October loadings at Tecar and Porto Sudeste fell to 8.90 Mt from 11.75 Mt a year earlier, a reduction of 2.85 Mt. The decline highlights a weaker source of conventional Capesize cargo demand alongside the larger nominated programmes at Vale’s ports. Anglo American reported Minas-Rio production of 6.3 Mt in the third quarter, up 24% year on year. Samarco reported production of 4.3 Mt, up 4%. However, sales declined 5% to 3.9 Mt. Separately, Signal Ocean Platform’s Dry Bulk Flows records show that Açu’s China-bound shipments increased to 9.18 Mt in January–September from 5.15 Mt a year earlier. Ubu shipped only 0.37 Mt to China over the same period, with South Korea, Egypt and the US among its main destinations. The stronger China-bound flow from Açu therefore has a more direct connection to Brazil–China vessel employment than Samarco’s production recovery. For freight, lower shipments at Tecar and Porto Sudeste may constrain spot Capesize enquiry, while increased Açu–China volumes support long-haul employment. Sustained support for C3 will depend on scheduled cargoes materialising and conventional Capesize demand absorbing available Atlantic tonnage. Vale’s Northern System performance, independent producer restarts, Chinese buying and ballast arrivals remain the main indicators to watch. articles.body: Ship Recycling Retains Its Stable Prospects in Hellenic Shipping News 05/11/2026 T he ship recycling market has remained stable over the past week. In its latest weekly report, Best Oasis ( www.best-oasis.com ), a leading cash buyer of ships, said that “the Indian ship recycling market remained relatively quiet during the week, with limited trading activity amid the festive period. Market participants are closely monitoring developments in the European Union, as the European Parliament’s Environment Committee is scheduled to vote on 4 November 2026 on a motion opposing the proposed inclusion of two Indian ship recycling yards in the EU-approved list. Vessel availability remains limited, with few suitable recycling candidates currently entering the market. Overall, market sentiment remains stable, with buying interest continuing despite subdued activity and limited vessel availability”. Source: Best Oasis According to Best Oasis, “the Bangladeshi ship recycling market continues to demonstrate strong buying interest, with buyers actively seeking suitable vessels for recycling. A recent bulk carrier sale reportedly concluded in the USD 540/LDT range on a delivered Bangladesh basis, reflecting firm buyer appetite and stronger price expectations. The recent transaction has contributed to an upward revision in prevailing market price indications, reflecting firmer pricing sentiment. Overall, market sentiment remains positive, supported by competitive buying interest despite the continued shortage of available tonnage. The Pakistani ship recycling market remained largely unchanged during the week, with buyers continuing to express interest in acquiring suitable vessels. Vessel availability remains extremely limited, restricting transaction activity despite continued buying interest. The domestic steel market remains under pressure due to weak demand, with no significant improvement in local market conditions reported during the week. Overall, market sentiment remains mixed, with sustained buying interest offset by subdued domestic demand and limited vessel availability. Finally, the Turkish ship recycling market remains stable, with limited trading activity and no significant changes reported during the week. The Turkish lira continues to remain weak, although currency fluctuations have not resulted in any further impact on recycling prices for the time being. Vessel availability remains influenced by EU regulations and the supply of suitable recycling candidates trading within or positioned near the region. Overall, Turkish recycling yards remain relatively busy and selective in their purchasing approach, with buying interest primarily focused on well-positioned and commercially attractive vessels that meet their specific requirements”, Best Oasis’ report concluded. Meanwhile, in a separate note, shipbroker Intermodal said that “last week, ship recycling conditions were relatively stable, with mixed sentiment across the main destinations. Bangladesh stood out stronger, while India and Pakistan held steady, as recyclers kept a selective approach. Alang’s sentiment remained unchanged, as the festive season continued to weigh on trading activity. Local steel prices declined, as steel demand remained sluggish. The Indian rupee edged higher against the USD, supported by RBI’s liquidity tightening measures, ahead of interest rate hike expectations to combat inflation. Source: Intermodal Few suitable LNG and tanker recycling candidates have been circulated to the market, as recyclers maintained their selective approach. Chattogram firmed, with competitive buying interest emerging, despite limited supply of vessels. Local steel prices rose slightly, as the market returned from holidays with little momentum. Local currency weakened against the USD. Limited candidates were circulated, as yards were busy with ongoing commitments. On the policy front, authorized recycling facilities increased to 39 and the national ship recycling industry has been upgraded from red to orange environmental category. Gadani was quiet. However, there was cautious interest in acquiring suitable tonnage, amid supply shortage. Local steel market stayed subdued, with steel prices declining. Local currency saw little changes, as it slightly gained against the USD. A few bulk carriers were circulated, but breakers showed limited appetite. On the economy side, the central bank raised interest rates by 50 basis points to 12%, as inflation rose to 11.32% y-o-y. Aliaga continued to see limited trading activity. Local steel prices are expected to increase as steel demand picks up, despite the two-day national holiday”, Intermodal concluded. articles.title: NAPA on why wind-assisted ships need proof of savings, not just a contract
articles.summary: BIMCO recently adopted its Energy Saving Device Retrofit Addendum in Autumn 2026, giving owners and charterers a contractual framework to agree how the cost, time and fuel savings of a retrofit are shared during a time charter. For wind-assisted propulsion systems (WAPS), it targets the obstacle most often cited for...
articles.body: NAPA on why wind-assisted ships need proof of savings, not just a contract in International Shipping News 05/11/2026 B IMCO recently adopted its Energy Saving Device Retrofit Addendum in Autumn 2026, giving owners and charterers a contractual framework to agree how the cost, time and fuel savings of a retrofit are shared during a time charter. For wind-assisted propulsion systems (WAPS), it targets the obstacle most often cited for slow uptake: the owner usually pays for the installation while the charterer keeps the fuel savings. A contract for sharing savings, however, only works if both parties can agree on what the savings were. That is where wind-assisted shipping still has a gap. Wind propulsion has moved well past the trial stage. According to the International Windship Association, more than 100 commercial ships now sail with wind propulsion fitted, totalling over six million deadweight tonnes, and around 100 more are on order. Retrofits are typically saving between 5% – 20% of fuel in service, with the variation dependent on trade route, prevailing winds and the size of the sails relative to the ship’s installed power. That spread is the commercial problem in a single figure: on any given voyage, how much of the saving came from the sails, and how much from good weather or a well-chosen route? Those numbers matter more each year as CII, FuelEU Maritime and the EU ETS raise the bar on efficiency and emissions. FuelEU Maritime already rewards wind directly, applying a multiplier to a vessel’s GHG intensity that is banded according to available effective wind power relative to propulsion power. The IMO Net-Zero Framework, which is still under discussion at the time of writing, would pair a fuel standard with emissions pricing and could have a similar impact worldwide. Knowing how much a WAPS contributes to a ship’s emissions profile is therefore part of knowing a fleet’s compliance exposure. Routing is a large part of the answer. For a conventional ship, wind is mostly an obstacle that adds resistance, rough seas and fuel burn. For a ship with rotor sails or wing-sails, it becomes a possible source of thrust, which can justify a longer track to reach a better wind speed and angle, or a slower passage to get more out of the sails. The best route will vary with the optimization objective, such as fuel saving, speed, arrival time, cost or profit, as well as with the weather, the ship and its wind system. Many weather routing tools were never built to do this. They treat the vessel’s performance as fixed and add wind as a simple extra push, rather than modelling how it interacts with waves, rudder angle, propeller and engine load at the same time. A credible approach maps wind along the whole route before departure, reassesses it against swell, wind waves and current, and states savings in dollars rather than percentages, so operators can see the financial case for a routing decision before committing to it. NAPA’s performance models start from the ship’s 3D hull form and hydrodynamics and are calibrated with operational data. That allows them to estimate what the vessel would have burned on the same voyage, in the same conditions, with no sails. This counterfactual baseline is what turns a claimed saving into a verifiable one – and it is the figure an owner and a charterer need in front of them when they divide the savings under a charter. The same model supports pre-installation simulation, routing in service and post-installation validation. Mikko Vartiainen, Wind Assisted Vessel Optimization Lead, NAPA The same evidence matters for compliance. FuelEU Maritime already rewards wind directly, applying a multiplier to a vessel’s GHG intensity that is banded according to available effective wind power relative to propulsion power. Under the EU ETS, every tonne of CO2 the sails avoid is an allowance the company does not have to surrender. The IMO Net-Zero Framework, which is still under discussion at the time of writing, would pair a fuel standard with emissions pricing and could have a similar impact worldwide. Knowing how much a WAPS contributes to a ship’s emissions profile is therefore part of knowing a fleet’s compliance exposure, not only its fuel bill. It also helps with the split incentive. Under time charters, the owner usually pays for the installation, and the charterer keeps the fuel savings, which is widely seen as the biggest structural obstacle to wider uptake. Voyage-level data that isolates the WAPS contribution from gains due to routing or weather gives both parties evidence to negotiate how savings are divided. Verification has limits, wind forecasts can shift quickly, so a route planned on a five-day forecast may lose its advantage as conditions change. Predicting sail performance in heavy seas is harder than in settled weather. And no model closes the distance between what a ship could theoretically achieve and what a crew, bound by schedule and charterer instructions, can realistically deliver. NAPA has developed a method for measuring what a WAPS has delivered using the vessel’s own signal data and a verified digital twin, during normal commercial operation rather than dedicated trials. The industry still lacks an agreed standard for in-service verification. BIMCO’s addendum gives owners and charterers a way to write a savings split into a charter. With one, ship and shore teams can work from the same picture, charterparties can be negotiated with confidence, and owners and operators can be sure their vessels meet regulatory requirements. A contract for sharing savings, however, only works if both parties can agree on what the savings were.
That is where wind-assisted shipping still has a gap.

articles.body: Baltic Dry Index Rebounds in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 05/11/2026 The Baltic Exchange’s dry bulk freight index, which tracks rates for ships carrying dry bulk commodities, jumped by 4% to 2,694 points on Wednesday, halting a two-day losing streak, supported by the larger vessels. The capesize index, which typically transports 150,000-ton cargoes, including iron ore and coal, also snapped a two-day losing streak, soaring by 7.2% to 4,097 points, likely tracking higher iron ore prices. articles.body: BIMCO: Coal shipments to India drop 7%, but limited recovery may lie ahead in Dry Bulk Market , Freight News , International Shipping News 05/11/2026 “B etween January and October, coal shipments to India dropped 7% y/y due to the increased cost of imports. Thermal coal demand has remained strong, particularly from the power sector, but domestic mining has not kept pace, forcing power plants to draw down inventories. In contrast, coking coal demand growth has eased following a decline in steel production amid low margins,” says Filipe Gouveia, Shipping Analysis Manager at BIMCO. The cost of imported coal has increased due to a weaker rupee and higher coal prices. Prices have firmed due to increased demand following disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. As LNG supplies have tightened, the EU, Japan and South Korea have boosted electricity generation from coal. Furthermore, Chinese imports increased at the end of the second quarter following a mining accident that led to mine closures for inspections and thus lower production. Indian coal demand has firmed this year, driven by an approximate 9% y/y increase in coal-fired electricity generation. While electricity generation from solar and wind has also increased, the impact on coal demand has been minimal as hydroelectric generation has fallen due to a weaker monsoon linked to El Niño conditions. While, domestic coal production has increased by only around 4% y/y, inventories, rather than imports, have compensated and supported demand growth. By 1 November, 48% of Indian coal-fired power plants had critically low coal inventories. “As the world’s second-largest coal importer, accounting for 17% of global coal shipments, India’s weaker import demand has weighed on the wider market. However, the impact has been particularly pronounced for the supramax segment, whose coal shipments to India have fallen 16% y/y. Panamaxes have fared better, with volumes falling only 4% y/y, as they increasingly competed with other ship segments for coal cargoes,” says Gouveia. However, after several months of weaker shipments, Indian coal import demand appears to have firmed, with shipments rising 7% y/y in October. Critically low inventories have likely increased pressure on power plants to secure sufficient coal supplies, while power shortages may have further encouraged purchasing. In the coming months, high electricity demand, paired with the need to rebuild inventories, could support India’s coal import demand. “Looking ahead, the International Energy Agency expects Indian coal demand to only grow by 2.5% in 2027. Although the country is expected to see rising electricity demand and industrial activity, a recovery in hydroelectric generation could limit gains. Indian coal imports are also expected to increase only slightly, as growing domestic coal mining may limit import demand,” says Gouveia. The issuing of General License 135 on October 9, which temporarily allows Russian diesel to be imported to the U.S., has yet to result in any cargo being delivered to the U.S. Three Tankers Set Out for the U.S. With Russian Diesel Three tankers were flagged last month as sailing for the U.S. with diesel cargoes, including Russia-flagged TALISMAN (IMO 9292060), Sierra Leone-flagged LERUO (IMO 9385831) and Malta-flagged AGIOI FANENDES (IMO 9798375). The third tanker, which is Greece-owned, is not sanctioned and appears to be the only one on a trajectory that is likely to see a U.S. port discharge. Changing AIS Destinations Signal Shifting Plans TALISMAN has changed its AIS-declared destination of “Atlantic Coast FO” to “For Order” and has sailed through the Strait of Gibraltar. LERUO has also amended its AIS destination to “Brazil for order” from “Atlantic coast for order”, also signaling an amendment of its original U.S. plans. The AGIOI FANENDES is similarly circumspect. After originally signaling New York, the tanker is now signaling “for orders” but appears to be sailing for the northeast U.S. coast still. articles.title: World’s first green ammonia-powered iron ore shipment leaves Western Australia
articles.summary: The dry-bulker Mineral Europa, owned by CMB.TECH and chartered by Fortescue, has left Port Hedland, bunkered with green ammonia and carrying a shipment of iron ore heading for China. A landmark achievement was reached this week on one of the world’s most important commodity trade routes when Mineral Europa left Port...
articles.body: World’s first green ammonia-powered iron ore shipment leaves Western Australia in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 05/11/2026 The dry-bulker Mineral Europa, owned by CMB.TECH and chartered by Fortescue, has left Port Hedland, bunkered with green ammonia and carrying a shipment of iron ore heading for China. A landmark achievement was reached this week on one of the world’s most important commodity trade routes when Mineral Europa left Port Hedland in Western Australia following a successful ship-to-ship green ammonia bunker trial and loading of iron ore. Mineral Europa was delivered by a Chinese shipyard in early October and completed the world’s first commercial ship-to-ship green ammonia bunkering operation off the port of Zhoushan, China, before setting course towards Port Hedland. The ammonia-powered voyage, laden with a commercial shipment of iron ore, was made possible by the significant investments of Pilbara Ports Authority, Fortescue, and CMB.TECH. This milestone demonstrates the power of collaboration across the full value chain—from mining and shipping to ports, fuel suppliers, and engine technology providers. Port Hedland is one of several ports operated by Pilbara Ports. If the transport of iron ore from the Pilbara were powered solely by low-carbon ammonia, those emissions would be cut by around 94%, from 9.9 million tonnes CO2 equivalent per year to less than 0.6 million tonnes. The achievement is a pivotal step in decarbonising the Australia-East Asia iron ore trade route, made even more impressive by occurring significantly earlier than the 2028 deployment target set out in the corridor’s 2023 feasibility study. Needs policy support To move beyond this demonstration and scale up zero- or near-zero-emission-fuelled shipping, the industry needs policies that help to address the remaining cost gap between these fuels and their conventional counterparts. While leading companies are starting to invest in e-fuels, such as clean ammonia in this case, broader adoption requires mechanisms that de-risk investments and help e-fuels reach commercial scale. “To avoid losing momentum, policy support is critical for industry members. This could be measures that can help spur clean fuel demand, reduce the fuel cost gap, and help ensure the build-up and availability of necessary fuel and port infrastructure,” says Jesse Fahnestock, director of decarbonisation at the Global Maritime Forum. Examples include contracts for difference, double-auction mechanisms, and capital grants for port and bunkering infrastructure, according to Fahnestock. The Global Maritime Forum has convened the Australia-East Asia iron ore green corridor initiative since 2022. Pilbara Ports Authority and Fortescue are among the 14 members involved in the initiative. Source: Global Maritime Forum 2026-11-05 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Lloyd’s Register launches service to manage cargo disruptions
articles.summary: Lloyd’s Register (LR) Advisory has launched a new Supply Chain Resilience service to help ports, governments and logistics operators manage cargo disruptions and identify alternative transport routes. The service was introduced on 4 November 2026 at the IAPH World Ports Conference in London. It focuses on keeping...
articles.body: Lloyd’s Register (LR) Advisory has launched a new Supply Chain Resilience service to help ports, governments and logistics operators manage cargo disruptions and identify alternative transport routes. The service was introduced on 4 November 2026 at the IAPH World Ports Conference in London. It focuses on keeping essential cargo moving when geopolitical tensions, port congestion, severe weather or infrastructure failures affect established trade routes. According to LR, disruptions at major ports or transport corridors can create delays across wider logistics networks. As a result, alternative gateways may face additional pressure, while road and rail connections struggle to handle diverted cargo. The new service aims to help organisations assess these risks and prepare practical responses before disruptions spread. Alternative routes and disruption planning LR Advisory examines transport networks across ports, airports, road borders and rail connections. It then assesses alternative routes based on available capacity, costs, delays and operational risks. The service also evaluates different transport combinations, including sea-air, sea-land and air-land connections. During the first 90 days of a disruption, LR can assess affected routes and develop a response plan covering 30, 60 and 90 days. These plans may include cargo prioritisation, alternative routing, additional transport capacity and operational measures to manage changing conditions. For time-sensitive shipments, such as food, medicines and industrial materials, the service helps operators determine which cargo should receive priority. Kamran Ul Haq, Senior Vice President of LR Ports Advisory, said choosing an alternative port does not automatically resolve supply chain problems. He explained that operators must also consider inland transport capacity, border procedures and the additional costs of diverting cargo. Long-term supply chain resilience Beyond immediate disruption management, LR Advisory also supports longer-term transport and infrastructure planning. The service can assess logistics networks over periods ranging from three months to five years. This includes identifying opportunities to reduce reliance on individual ports and trade corridors. Furthermore, LR can evaluate potential investments in dry ports, inland logistics hubs and rail-connected freight facilities. According to the company, these assessments aim to improve network flexibility and strengthen cargo flows during future disruptions. The new service combines short-term contingency planning with longer-term infrastructure assessments, helping logistics operators prepare for changing conditions across international supply chains.

On October 29, 2026, a Somali Pirate Action Group of 12 armed pirates hijacked the Iranian fishing dhow AZINI approximately 185 nautical miles east of Bandarbeyla, Puntland. The vessel’s crew reportedly included 21 Iranian fishermen and two Somali security guards. On November 2, the Indian Navy freed the vessel following a 48-hour operation in the Arabian Sea, and all crew are reportedly safe. The hijacking of AZINI is the first confirmed hijacking of the fourth quarter and the fourth confirmed hijacking of a dhow or fishing vessel off Somalia this year. It follows a string of seizures that peaked in the spring. On January 1, the China-flagged LIAO DONG YU 578 (MMSI 412549025) was reportedly captured by pirates off Bandarbeyla while fishing, although official sources have not confirmed the hijacking. The Chinese Embassy in Somalia reported that a Chinese fishing vessel was released from pirate custody on March 2, but did not name the vessel. On March 24, a PAG seized the Iran-flagged fishing dhow ALWASEEMI 786 , which was abandoned under naval pressure on April 5. The fishing vessel ALKHARY 2 was hijacked on approximately April 20 and released on April 22. On April 25, a PAG seized the UAE-flagged dhow FAHAD 4 and reportedly used it as a mothership in an attempted attack on the MINERVA PISCES on April 28. The pirates then abandoned the dhow in the Arabian Sea on May 4 after their supplies ran short. An unnamed dhow was reportedly hijacked on May 9 while en route to Kismayo, and its current status is unknown. At least two unnamed Iranian dhows were also reportedly seized and released after a $40,000 ransom payment, although official sources have not confirmed these incidents. Why Attacks on Dhows Go Underreported Attacks on dhows and fishing vessels by PAGs off Somalia are likely underreported. Many of the Iranian dhows fishing in the region are part of an unregulated fleet that does not broadcast IMO numbers and frequently operates with AIS off, a practice that may also serve as a defensive measure against piracy. These vessels are also low-value targets. They command far smaller ransoms than merchant vessels, so their seizures draw less attention than attacks on commercial shipping. The confirmed count is very likely a floor rather than a full picture. Why Pirates Target Fishing Vessels Pirates are likely targeting fishing vessels for two reasons. Motherships Extend Pirate Range Toward Shipping Lanes Dhows and fishing vessels can be used as motherships that extend the range of PAGs far offshore and toward major shipping lanes. The Maritime Security Centre Indian Ocean (MSCIO) highlighted this risk following the AZINI hijacking. The FAHAD 4 case shows the threat in practice, since pirates used the dhow to attempt an attack on a merchant vessel three days after seizing it. Resentment Over Illegal Fishing Illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing by foreign fleets is a documented driver of attacks on fishing vessels. Pirates involved in the seizure of foreign fishing vessels have cited resentment against illegal fishers as the reason for their attacks.

articles.title: Port of Oakland reports considerable renewable and zero-carbon electricity supply
articles.summary: The Port of Oakland has announced that 84% of the electricity delivered in 2025 by its publicly owned utility, Port Public Power, to port tenants and facilities came from renewable and zero-carbon sources. The Board of Commissioners approved the annual Power Source Disclosure Report and Power Content Label for...
articles.body: The Port of Oakland has announced that 84% of the electricity delivered in 2025 by its publicly owned utility, Port Public Power, to port tenants and facilities came from renewable and zero-carbon sources. The Board of Commissioners approved the annual Power Source Disclosure Report and Power Content Label for submission to the California Energy Commission at its October 22 meeting. Source: Port of Oakland Renewable resources made up 61% of the supply, against a 46% average for California utilities, with geothermal the largest source, followed by solar, biomass and biogas, and eligible small hydroelectric power. A further 21% came from large hydroelectric power, and other zero-carbon market purchases brought the combined share to 84%. The supply’s greenhouse gas intensity was 186 pounds of carbon dioxide equivalent per megawatt-hour, less than half the 384 pounds of the average California utility. Port Public Power expects demand on its system to grow four- to five-fold over the next five years as tenants electrify their operations, potentially reaching 100 megawatts. The port continues to modernise, expand and replace ageing electrical infrastructure to support this. In 2025 the Board approved a 20-year Energy Storage Service Agreement with Trolley Pass Project LLC, giving the port 4 megawatts of capacity at a battery storage facility in San Bernardino County, which can help it make better use of solar power and reduce reliance on market purchases. The port’s efforts support California’s Senate Bill 100 goal of 100 percent clean electricity by 2045, and as a member of the Northern California Power Agency it works with other public power utilities to secure reliable, affordable and sustainable supply. Andre Basler, Director of Utilities at the Port of Oakland, said that as more of the port runs on electricity, the aim is to keep that electricity clean, reliable and affordable, so tenants electrifying their trucks and equipment move onto one of the cleanest power supplies in California, and the port intends to keep making it cleaner as demand grows.

articles.title: Oil Prices Drop 9% After Republicans Lose Congress in Midterm Elections

articles.body: Oil Prices Drop 9% After Republicans Lose Congress in Midterm Elections Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 4, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Piya W. Oil prices fell 9% on Wednesday in volatile trading as investors awaited Washington's next move in the US-Israeli war with Iran after President Donald Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress in midterm elections. Brent futures dropped $9.27, or 8.9%, to $94.29 a barrel, touching the lowest level since September 4, at 11:58 a.m. ET (1658 GMT). US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $7.44, or 7.8%, to $88.54. Brent settled in the previous session at its lowest level in nearly four weeks as traders weighed talks to end wars in Ukraine and Iran. "Larger crude oil exports out of the Middle East, along with President Trump stating he has no immediate plans to strike Iran, is keeping the pressure on crude oil prices for now. The Democratic control of Congress could also tighten US military spending in the Middle East and further heighten the possibility of a peace deal sooner than later," said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at US financial services firm BOK Financial. Trump acknowledged that the Iran war had played a role in his party's sweeping defeat in the midterm elections, as Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday that the United States had no immediate plans to strike Iran. Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei said in a written statement that US hostility would persist regardless of which party was in power. Yemen's Houthis said they had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. There was no confirmation from Saudi authorities. QATAR SEEKS TO AVOID ESCALATION Qatar stepped up mediation efforts to avert an escalation of attacks after the US elections. A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday that Iran and the United States remain far from a deal to end their war. "The elections are giving bears a reason to cast doubt on a continuation in Iran ... I'm more concerned that we can see an escalation in Iran sooner than a resolution," said Carl Larry, who leads the trading and North America risk team at Enverus. Gulf exports of crude, condensate and refined products, excluding liquefied petroleum gas, averaged 17.1 million barrels per day in October, according to ship-tracking data from Vortexa, down from 18.9 million bpd in September but still roughly three-quarters of pre-war levels. The United Arab Emirates is considering a third oil-export pipeline that would deliver crude outside the Strait of Hormuz, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter, as the country aims to sharply reduce its dependence on the waterway. In the US, crude stocks, gasoline and distillate inventories fell last week, the Energy Information Administration said. Crude inventories fell by 865,000 barrels to 409.8 million barrels in the week ended October 30, the EIA said, compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for an 877,000-barrel rise. (Reuters)

articles.title: Transpacific emerges as liner shipping’s golden trade
articles.summary: The transpacific has become the most lucrative major container shipping trade in the world, with carriers generating five times more spot revenue per nautical mile on the Shanghai–Los Angeles route than on shipments to North Europe via the Cape of Good Hope. New analysis from Alphaliner shows that the extraordinary...
articles.body: Containers Transpacific emerges as liner shipping’s golden trade Sam Chambers November 5, 2026 0 1 1 minute read Port of Long Beach Port of Long Beach The transpacific has become the most lucrative major container shipping trade in the world, with carriers generating five times more spot revenue per nautical mile on the Shanghai–Los Angeles route than on shipments to North Europe via the Cape of Good Hope. New analysis from Alphaliner shows that the extraordinary strength of the US trade has persisted well beyond the traditional peak season, with freight rates approaching levels last seen during the pandemic. At approximately $7,500 per feu, the 5,775 nautical mile Shanghai–Los Angeles voyage generates $1.30 in revenue per container per nautical mile, compared with just 26 cents on Shanghai–Rotterdam via the Cape, or 34 cents via Suez. Shanghai–New York generates 96 cents per nautical mile, with spot rates remaining above $10,000 per feu since late August. These figures represent revenue rather than profit, but nevertheless illustrate the extraordinary divergence between the industry’s principal east–west trades. Carriers are responding by throwing more tonnage at the Pacific. MSC recently upgraded its Sentosa service with 23,600 teu megamaxes, replacing vessels of approximately 15,000 teu. ZIM, which already deploys 52% of its capacity on the Pacific, will launch another China–California service in December. The boom is feeding directly into corporate earnings. COSCO reported third-quarter liner profits of $2.66bn, double the year-earlier level, with transpacific revenue surging 61.2%. Freightos confirms that the transpacific’s extraordinary resilience has continued into November. Its latest assessment places Asia–US west coast rates at $8,340 per feu and east coast rates at $9,911. Freightos noted that rates remain approximately $5,500 per feu above pre-peak-season levels, while the approaching Lunar New Year demand cycle could limit the extent of any correction. However, signs of cooling are emerging. Drewry reported Shanghai–Los Angeles rates falling 6% to $7,514 last week, with Shanghai–New York declining 5% to $9,631. The consultancy expects further weakness as US ocean imports are forecast to decline 11% month-on-month in November. Meanwhile, Sea-Intelligence has warned that transpacific capacity deployment is reaching unprecedented levels. Weekly Asia–US west coast capacity is expected to hit 400,000 teu in November, although congestion and delayed departures are inflating the figures. Photo: Department of War The United States on Wednesday sanctioned a network of individuals and companies accused of operating fraudulent ship registries that helped Iran’s shadow fleet evade sanctions, while issuing a new warning to maritime companies about the risks of dealing with falsely flagged vessels. The U.S. Treasury Department announced the sanctions on Wednesday as part of Operation Economic Outcast, targeting an India-based network led by Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid. According to Treasury, the couple operated a network of fraudulent flag registries and maritime certification services that allowed sanctioned tankers carrying Iranian petroleum to continue operating under flags they were not legally authorized to fly. Some of those vessels were transporting oil on behalf of Iran’s military and its proxies, Treasury said. The network allegedly impersonated maritime authorities in countries including Guyana, Eswatini, Laos, Aruba, Nicaragua, and Sint Maarten, issuing registration documents and certifications without authorization from the governments involved. In many cases, the operation relied on websites designed to look like legitimate national ship registries, offering everything from vessel registration to seafarer certification and classification services. Treasury said the scheme dates back to at least 2014, when Sharma and Shahid sought to impersonate the flag administration of Dominica. In 2023, Sharma established Singapore-based Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry PTE Ltd., which continued providing registration services for vessels transporting Iranian oil even after authorities in Eswatini publicly disavowed the operation. Among the vessels identified by Treasury was the sanctioned tanker PING SHUN (IMO 9231901), which had previously transported multiple shipments of Iranian oil. The network also allegedly provided false flags to sanctioned tankers LATTAFA (IMO 9245794), BINARY STAR (IMO 9380570), and VERA (IMO 9304655). Treasury cited the case of the MAJESTIC X , formerly PHONIX (IMO 9198317), which was seized by U.S. military forces on April 22 while carrying Iranian oil. The tanker had been operating under a fraudulent Guyana flag. The sanctions target Sharma, Shahid, two associates, and nine companies and organizations linked to the network, including Oceaniek Technologies India, Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited, and Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry. OFAC Warns Maritime Industry Over False Flags Alongside the designations, the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new industry alert warning that companies providing services to vessels operating under fraudulent flags could face sanctions or penalties. The warning reflects a growing problem in the shadow fleet trade, where vessels increasingly rely on questionable or outright fraudulent registrations after being removed from legitimate flag registries. OFAC said that while shadow fleet operators have long used frequent flag changes to obscure their activities, fraudulent registries have become an increasingly common way to keep sanctioned vessels operating. These registries can create the appearance of legitimate registration even when the country whose flag is being used has never authorized the vessel to fly it. OFAC urged insurers, financial institutions, and other maritime service providers to conduct additional due diligence when dealing with vessels showing signs of false registration. Among the warning signs identified by OFAC are vessels with unknown flags, registration documents that cannot be verified, and discrepancies between a ship’s reported flag and the country code associated with its Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) number. The agency also warned about vessels claiming flags from countries without recognized ship registries. The implications extend beyond sanctions compliance. Flag states are responsible for overseeing vessel safety, certification, and compliance with international maritime regulations. Vessels operating under fraudulent registrations may lack legitimate regulatory oversight and valid insurance coverage. Treasury warned that falsely flagged vessels could expose coastal nations to billions of dollars in potential environmental and economic damages in the event of a major maritime casualty. OFAC also encouraged governments to investigate fraudulent registries operating in their names and report suspected cases to the International Maritime Organization so that maritime databases accurately reflect vessels with invalid registrations. Broader Pressure on Iran The measures are part of Operation Economic Outcast, a sanctions campaign launched in August aimed at cutting off the financial networks supporting Iran’s oil exports and other economic activities. The latest action comes as the United States continues its maritime blockade of Iran amid the ongoing war, with Washington seeking to disrupt the networks that allow Iranian oil to reach international markets. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that companies and individuals continuing to support the Iranian government would face consequences. “We know where you are, and we will sanction those who continue supporting the Iranian regime, whether by land, sea, or air,” Bessent said. The sanctions package also included Türkiye-based Fugo Ground Services Inc., which Treasury said continued providing ground handling services to several sanctioned Iranian airlines. The maritime designations and new OFAC advisory highlight Washington’s growing focus on the service providers and intermediaries that keep Iran’s shadow fleet operating, rather than the tankers themselves. articles.body: Rhenus has reported a 26% year-on-year increase in ocean freight volumes from China to Europe during 2026 to date, as the logistics provider expands its business along the trade corridor. The company recorded the growth despite changing capacity conditions and uncertainty surrounding EU-China trade policies. According to Rhenus, the China-Europe corridor is its largest ocean freight trade lane when volumes in both directions are combined. The increase reflects the company’s efforts to strengthen customer relationships and coordinate freight movements between its Asian and European operations. Renee Toh, Global Head of Ocean Freight at Rhenus, said closer cooperation between regional teams and carrier partners helps the company understand customer requirements and improve transport planning. Meanwhile, Rhenus continues to manage challenges linked to uneven cargo flows between China and Europe. Changes in available shipping capacity and trade policies also influence transport decisions across the corridor. Air freight volumes also increase Alongside its ocean freight business, Rhenus reported growth in air cargo movements between China and Europe. New customer contracts supported higher China-to-Europe air freight volumes despite weaker conditions in parts of the market. The company also recorded approximately 20% growth in air freight volumes from Europe to China. According to market data cited by Rhenus from Rotate, overall Europe-to-China air freight demand declined by 5% year on year during January–August 2026. In addition, the company identified high-tech cargo as one of its fastest-growing air freight segments on the China-Europe route. Chris Bode, Vice President of Air Freight at Rhenus, said the company is focusing on industries where specialised logistics expertise can support customer requirements. Rhenus currently operates 16 offices across Greater China, employing more than 550 people. These operations connect with its wider European network to support international freight movements. Its air freight gateways in Shanghai and Hong Kong provide cargo consolidation and handling services. Meanwhile, customs brokerage, warehousing and inland transport services support local collection and distribution. The company announced the figures ahead of the China International Import Expo, scheduled to take place in Shanghai from 5 to 10 November 2026.

SAUL LOEB/Pool via REUTERS/File Photo Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday blamed Republicans’ midterm election losses on the Trump administration’s eight-month war with Iran, which has driven up global energy prices and left commercial shipping under continued threat in the Strait of Hormuz. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote on X , a day after Democrats won control of both the House and Senate. Vance argued that the results reflected growing frustration with the war, rather than simply a failure by Republicans to turn out their voters. He cited internal polling showing four major concerns among voters: ending the Iran war, inflation and the cost of living, putting America first, and the United States’ relationship with Israel. The remarks are notable coming from the vice president of an administration that launched the war in February and has spent much of the year defending its military campaign. As recently as September, Vance resisted calling the conflict a war, telling reporters at a White House briefing that major combat operations had already ended. “I wouldn’t call it a war,” he said at the time. Vance also said Washington would not return to negotiations with Tehran until Iran stopped attacking commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. President Donald Trump has also acknowledged that the war contributed to Republicans’ election losses, although he defended his decision to launch the military campaign. “I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” Trump told The Wall Street Journal. The comments come as the administration faces growing pressure over the war’s economic consequences, including higher fuel prices and continued disruptions to global shipping. The war, launched by the United States and Israel on February 28, has left the Strait of Hormuz at the center of a prolonged military and economic standoff. The United States has maintained a blockade targeting Iranian maritime commerce, while Iran has continued attacking merchant ships in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf. Although tanker traffic has recovered considerably from the early months of the conflict, the security situation remains volatile. Several new maritime incidents were reported over the weekend, including attacks on tankers and other commercial vessels. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) issued additional warnings this week, highlighting the continued danger to merchant shipping despite U.S. efforts to secure the waterway. The disruption has driven up tanker rates, war-risk insurance costs, and global energy prices. Brent crude has remained above $100 a barrel, while higher gasoline and diesel prices have added to concerns about the cost of living in the United States. The election results now add another layer of uncertainty over the future of the conflict. With Democrats set to take control of Congress in January, the administration could face greater scrutiny of its military strategy, the continued blockade of Iranian shipping, and the economic costs of the war. Congress controls defense spending and could pursue legislation seeking to limit military operations, although Trump would retain substantial executive authority and the ability to veto legislation. For the shipping industry, the immediate questions remain whether Washington will continue its current approach, resume major combat operations, or reach an agreement with Tehran that could reduce threats to commercial vessels. Vance’s remarks come as the White House weighs those options, with the vice president now publicly blaming the administration’s own war for Republicans’ loss of Congress. articles.body: GXO Logistics reported higher revenue and net income for the third quarter of 2026, supported by stronger organic growth and an increase in new business contracts. The company generated revenue of US$3.6 billion, up 5.7% from US$3.4 billion a year earlier. Organic revenue grew by 6.4%, marking its fastest expansion in more than three years. Meanwhile, net income increased to US$65 million from US$60 million in the same quarter of 2025. Adjusted earnings per share also rose to US$0.89 from US$0.79. However, adjusted EBITDA remained unchanged at US$251 million, despite the increase in revenue. New logistics contracts support growth GXO secured US$375 million in new business wins during the quarter, representing a 34% increase year over year. This marked the second consecutive quarter in which new contract wins grew by more than 30%. As a result, year-to-date new business wins exceeded US$1 billion, approaching the total recorded throughout 2025. The company’s sales pipeline also reached a record US$3.1 billion, increasing by more than 30% compared with the previous year. Approximately 40% of new business wins during the first nine months came from GXO’s strategic growth sectors. These include aerospace and defence, technology, industrial operations and life sciences. Patrick Kelleher, Chief Executive Officer of GXO, said the company’s strategy was supporting faster organic growth and stronger contract activity. He also highlighted improvements in operational execution, particularly in North America. In addition, GXO continues to introduce a unified labour management system and expand the deployment of its GXO IQ technology platform. GXO maintains full-year outlook Despite stronger revenue growth, GXO reported lower operating cash flow during the quarter. Cash generated from operations declined to US$156 million from US$232 million a year earlier. Free cash flow also decreased to US$85 million, compared with US$187 million in the third quarter of 2025. Nevertheless, the company reaffirmed its financial guidance for the full year. GXO continues to expect organic revenue growth of 4% to 5% in 2026. It also forecasts adjusted EBITDA between US$945 million and US$965 million. Meanwhile, adjusted diluted earnings per share are expected to range from US$2.95 to US$3.15. The company ended September with US$340 million in cash and cash equivalents, alongside total outstanding debt of US$2.8 billion. Looking ahead, GXO will present its longer-term strategy and financial outlook during its Investor Day on 16 November 2026.

Before then, MIOC detected only seven AIS-transmitting tankers loading almost 6 million barrels between July 27 and September 17, a pace of around 113,000 barrels per day. Satellite imagery points the same way. Automated detection over Kharg Island from September 18 to November 1 found no dark tanker at either of the island’s loading terminals. Dark vessels are holding the same nine positions in the anchorage east of Kharg Island, where tankers wait to load at Kharg. Spare Capacity Sits Unused Inside the Gulf Windward data shows 47 tankers in the Middle East Gulf that are owned by the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) or the National Iranian Tanker Company (NITC), fly Iran’s flag, or have made Iranian port calls in 2026. Only 25 of them still broadcast AIS, and 22 are dark, 14 of them since the blockade began. The figures that follow describe only the 25 tankers still transmitting, not Iran’s entire commercial tanker fleet. Of those 25, 15 (60%) appear to be in ballast, and 11 of them are VLCCs. Together they have nearly 24 million barrels of empty capacity. Another nine, including three VLCCs, sit laden with about 11 million barrels aboard. The load state of one is undetermined. Iran’s AIS-transmitting tankers in the Gulf have room to spare, but none of them has loaded since September 17. Three Explanations for Where the Crude Is Going There is no evidence showing where Iran’s crude is going instead, which leaves three possible explanations. The first is that crude is moving into onshore tanks at Kharg Island. The second is that tankers are loading while dark, between satellite passes. Either would only postpone the problem of Iran having limited capacity to keep its crude. The third is that Iran has cut output and begun capping wells. This would be its worst case, since it would risk equipment damage, add repair time, and raise the cost of bringing the wells back online. Iran’s Old Floating Storage Now Sits Empty Outside the Middle East Gulf, the AIS-visible tankers that once served as Iran’s floating storage prior to delivering their cargo now sit largely empty. Windward data shows 140 Iran-linked tankers broadcasting AIS outside the Gulf, of which 115 are in ballast, and 25 are laden. Five main holding areas account for 76 of those tankers, off Malaysia’s Eastern Outer Port Limits, Sri Lanka, eastern Malaysia, Karachi, and Duqm. Only three of the 76 are laden or partly laden, according to available AIS draft data. Laden AIS-transmitting Iran-associated tankers across Asia and the Indian Ocean carry about 9.6 million barrels. About 5.9 million barrels of that, or 61%, is in transit aboard five tankers heading toward China. What to Watch Each of the three explanations leaves a trace. A tanker anchored east of Kharg that changes position or draft between satellite passes would point to dark loading. Continued silence at the terminals would put more weight on onshore storage and, as those tanks fill, on output cuts. The longer the gap runs past six weeks, the narrower Iran’s options become.

REUTERS/Toby Melville/File Photo, Reuters By Archie Hunter and Alex Longley (Bloomberg) — As lawyers for Mercuria Energy Group presented the commodity giant’s case against the Baltic Exchange this week, a group of smartly dressed Norwegian businessmen listened intently to the arguments from the back of a packed London courtroom. The executives, representing Oslo-listed Hunter Group ASA, have around $100 million riding on the outcome. The company is in a dispute with Mercuria over a charter deal linked to the TD3C index — the global benchmark oil tanker rate that the trading house claims the Baltic Exchange should have suspended because of disruptions caused by the Iran war. Mercuria has been making reduced payments, leaving it in breach of contract and with arrears building, according to Hunter. “As of now, it’s more than $100 million total accrued charter income, losses and interest,” Hunter Chairman Morten Astrup told Bloomberg News in a London interview. A spokesperson for Mercuria declined to comment. Hunter’s unpaid bill highlights the billions of dollars in criss-crossing contracts that could be affected by a ruling in the London court. The case centers on whether it was still valid for the Baltic Exchange to continue publishing rates to ship oil from inside the Persian Gulf to China in the months after the Iran war broke out. The disputed TD3C rate relies on broker assessments of the cost of sending a supertanker to China from Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura. However, it also underpins other contracts between tanker owners and their customers as well as billions of dollars in derivatives. Mercuria says the Baltic Exchange should have suspended the benchmark rate from early March to July 3, when oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz came to a near standstill as Tehran targeted shipping in the waterway linking the Persian Gulf to the rest of the world. The Baltic Exchange, which plays a central role in setting global shipping rates, maintains that it was still possible to put a price on the freight risk using broker assessments, even after oil shipments through Hormuz were severely disrupted in the months following the start of the war. Since then, the prices for leasing crude-carrying supertankers climbed to record highs of well over $1 million a day as firms shuttled cargoes under fire from rockets and drones out of Hormuz. Surging rates saw Oslo-based Hunter’s second-quarter profit jump 13-fold to $47 million from a year earlier. The company, which previously owned and operated supertankers, now focuses on chartering vessels. Its shares have surged 882% this year to give Hunter a market value of about $255 million. Hunter benefited from its deal with Mercuria because it leased a vessel from the trading house at a fixed rate and then leased it back to Mercuria at a floating benchmark that has soared. Hunter hasn’t named Mercuria in its exchange filings, but said on Oct. 9 that an unnamed contractual counterpart owed it an outstanding $67.8 million as of the end of September. That should have increased as charter rates continued to rise in October. The vessel in question is a 10-year-old tanker named DHT Puma, which Mercuria took on a time charter from DHT Holdings Inc. until the first quarter of 2027. Mercuria then leased the DHT Puma to Hunter at a fixed level of $52,000 a day, according to evidence heard in court this week. It leased the vessel back from Hunter at a floating rate linked to the disputed TD3C index that’s jumped since the start of the war. In its second-quarter results, Hunter said its average time charter margin — the difference between the fixed rate and the spot rate during the period — was $401,172 a day. Ships are often traded multiple times between owners and chartering companies. Sometimes a vessel owner will hire out a ship at a fixed rate on a long-term deal to guarantee revenues over a prolonged period, while companies moving significant quantities of oil then have guaranteed access to a tanker. Traders can ultimately continue to hire out ships to other companies if they deem it lucrative to do so. Hunter Chairman Astrup said Mercuria has subsequently hired out the DHT Puma to shipping tycoon Ga-Hyun Chung’s Sinokor Group, which has been influential in driving the key TD3C benchmark. Mercuria is urging the London court to declare that the Baltic Exchange breached its obligations, though the trading house has repeatedly changed the outcome it’s seeking since first filing the lawsuit. This week, after the case had begun, Mercuria said that rather than seeking a retrospective suspension or restatement of the index, it now only wants a judge to declare that the Baltic Exchange shouldn’t have continued publishing TD3C from March to July. Prior to that, the company had asked for the values published for TD3C since March to be declared as having no effect, and that the index should be retrospectively suspended. Mercuria, which accused the Baltic Exchange of pressurizing brokers to provide rate assessments, has also removed from its pleadings references to losses it says it has suffered. It has never sought compensation from the Baltic in the case . It’s not clear what the changes to Mercuria’s claims mean for the arbitration Hunter launched to recover the money it says it’s owed by the commodity trader. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Maritime Industry Urges Trump to Let Jones Act Waiver Expire November 15
articles.summary: The American Maritime Partnership (AMP) is urging President Donald Trump to allow the emergency Jones Act waiver to expire on November 15, warning that nearly eight months of exemptions have...
