Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Faraways/Shutterstock The American Maritime Partnership (AMP) is urging President Donald Trump to allow the emergency Jones Act waiver to expire on November 15, warning that nearly eight months of exemptions have failed to lower fuel prices while undermining investment in the U.S. maritime industry. In a letter sent to the White House on Election Day, November 3, AMP President Jennifer Carpenter argued that extending the waiver again would directly conflict with the administration’s stated goal of restoring American maritime dominance. “The waiver responded to an extraordinary energy disruption, but after eight months, the record is clear: continuation of the waiver threatens to curtail your ambitious agenda to unleash investment that will restore American maritime dominance,” the letter states. The appeal carries the backing of AMP’s leadership, representing a broad cross-section of the domestic maritime industry, including vessel operators, shipbuilders, dredging companies and maritime labor organizations. The organization’s board includes representatives from Crowley, Matson, Kirby, TOTE, Pasha Hawaii, and the American Waterways Operators, among others. The Trump administration first issued the waiver on March 17 in response to energy market disruptions caused by the war with Iran. The measure temporarily allows foreign-flagged vessels to transport certain cargoes between U.S. ports, an activity normally reserved for qualified American vessels under the Jones Act. The administration subsequently extended the waiver twice, most recently in August, when it introduced new requirements for reviewing individual foreign-vessel movements. Those changes require the Maritime Administration to determine whether qualified U.S. vessels are available before foreign ships can be authorized to carry domestic cargo. AMP acknowledged that the revised process has reduced foreign-vessel activity while allowing essential cargo to continue moving. However, the organization argues that even the narrower waiver is doing lasting damage to the industry. Among its central claims is that the waiver has provided little, if any, benefit to American consumers. According to AMP, published analyses have found no demonstrated reduction in retail fuel prices attributable to the waiver, with the maximum estimated effect on gasoline prices amounting to less than half a cent per gallon. The organization argues that allowing foreign vessels into domestic trades does nothing to resolve the underlying problems driving energy prices, including disrupted global shipping routes, constrained inventories and refining economics. AMP also raised concerns about the involvement of foreign shipping interests, claiming that more than 28% of reported waiver voyages involved vessels or companies directly linked to China. The letter specifically points to Chinese shipping giant COSCO and raises broader concerns about vessels operating in domestic trades with foreign crews, including Russian mariners. Perhaps the most significant concern raised in the letter is the impact on future maritime investment. AMP says industry participants have reported more than $2.6 billion in delayed investments involving new vessels and shipyard expansion. The organization also cites more than $700 million in planned Jones Act dredging vessel investments that have been deferred amid uncertainty surrounding the waiver. The figures are based on industry reports cited by AMP. The organization argues that shipowners and lenders need confidence in long-term domestic cargo demand before committing capital to vessels and infrastructure that may remain in service for decades. The letter follows growing scrutiny of the waiver from lawmakers and maritime labor organizations. As gCaptain reported last week , nine maritime labor organizations recently raised concerns about compliance with federal reporting requirements, immigration laws and the national defense justification for foreign-vessel movements. Those concerns have also drawn attention from congressional lawmakers, who have questioned whether the prolonged waiver remains consistent with the national defense authority under which it was issued. AMP maintains that allowing the current waiver to expire would not prevent the administration from responding to legitimate emergencies. The organization points to existing authority under 46 U.S.C. 501(b), which permits targeted waivers when national defense needs cannot be met by available U.S. vessels. The decision now rests with the Trump administration. Under current Customs and Border Protection guidance , cargo transported under the existing waiver must be loaded before 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on November 15. For AMP, the approaching deadline presents an opportunity for the administration to demonstrate that its support for American shipbuilding extends to protecting the domestic market on which the industry depends. “Let American mariners carry American cargo. Let American shipyards build the vessels America needs. Let American investment strengthen American maritime power,” Carpenter wrote. articles.title: Trump Plays Down Prospect of Iran Strikes After Midterm Rout
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump said he has no immediate plans to launch strikes on Iran following midterm elections in which the Democrats took control of Congress in a landslide win over his Republican party.

U.S. Central Command said more than 20 U.S. Navy warships and hundreds of military aircraft are supporting the renewed maritime blockade of vessels traveling to and from Iranian ports. (U.S. Central Command photo) By Omar Tamo, Eltaf Najafizada and Fiona MacDonald (Bloomberg) — US President Donald Trump said he has no immediate plans to launch strikes on Iran following midterm elections in which the Democrats took control of Congress in a landslide win over his Republican party. Still, the next few weeks will be key, with Trump either being chastened by the election results — which laid bare the strong anti- Iran war sentiment among Americans — or thinking he needs to act before the new Congress members take office in early January. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” Trump said in an interview with the Financial Times about the conflict, though he added the US is still prepared for an escalation with the Islamic Republic if necessary. “I’m ready, we’re ready. We’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it.” Later, Trump said the war — now into its ninth month — wasn’t a primary reason for the Republicans being routed, despite Americans balking at the resulting surge in energy prices. “People understood the importance of what I’ve done with Iran,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News. “You can’t let the number one state sponsor of terror have a nuclear weapon. It’s the most dangerous country in the world, and we wiped them out practically. Haven’t finished a job, and maybe I will, and maybe I won’t.” Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and a senior negotiator with the US, said the midterms showed Americans have voted “NO TO WAR.” He warned the US of a “nightmare” if it does opt to restart mass attacks on Iran. While Trump and officials such as Vice President JD Vance have sounded slightly more dovish about Iran this week, sending oil prices lower, tensions between the warring sides are still high. Tehran has said it’s prepared for strikes to start at any moment and that it will retaliate fiercely. “The midterms just delivered a clear political signal against the war, but the next several weeks carry a high risk of military escalation before the new Congress is sworn in,” said Hamad Althunayyan, a political scientist at Kuwait University and research fellow at Harvard. “After January, blame-shifting between the president and Congress on the Iran war is the most predictable outcome.” Gulf Arab states are nervous and appealing to Trump to give diplomacy more time. American allies such as the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Saudi Arabia were attacked thousands of times by Iranian drones and missiles during the most intense phase of the war between late February and a truce in early April.Play Video Talks between Iran and the US, mediated by Qatar and Pakistan, have made little progress in recent weeks. Still, Qatari officials expect feedback from both sides to new proposals over the next day or so, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. The two countries are divided on a number of issues, with Iran wanting the US to lift a naval blockade on its ports and Washington seeking concessions on Tehran’s nuclear activities. Oil prices were down again on Wednesday, with Brent trading almost 2% lower to $101.70 a barrel. While it’s still up almost 70% this year, mostly because of the war and Iran’s attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, some traders think the Democrats’ wins will put pressure on Trump to avoid escalation. “The big question now is what lies ahead on the foreign policy front and specifically the Middle East crisis,” said Ole Sloth Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank AS. “The market seems to be betting Trump wants to put it behind him, raising the prospect for some sort of deal.” This week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government has been granted more authority by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to pursue peace talks. That could include issues previously considered “non-negotiable” by Tehran, Pezeshkian said. The war began in late February when the US and Israel attacked Iranian targets and killed senior officials, including former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. US officials initially talked of a war lasting no more than four to six weeks and Trump has grown frustrated with Iran’s resilience. Tehran has caused chaos across the Persian Gulf region and wider Middle East with its counterstrikes. The rise in fuel costs, with diesel hitting a record in the US and gasoline surpassing $4 a gallon on average, contributed significantly to Americans turning against the conflict. “The situation could go either way,” said Arman Mahmoudian, a research fellow at the University of South Florida. “Given that the scale of the Republicans’ electoral defeat appears to have exceeded expectations, Trump may either become more aggressive, believing he has little left to lose, or adopt a more cautious approach to avoid further weakening his political standing.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. The contract is worth more than EUR 7.9 million and has an implementation period of 24 months from the date of award. The tender specifications set the basic terms for contracting the service for the 2027-2029 period. The successful bidder will manage a platform intended to improve the competitiveness and coordination of all port community members and of the activities each one carries out. Information flows at Valenciaport are complex: every movement of goods requires multiple communications among many stakeholders, creating a dense network of exchanges, and the platform is meant to keep pace with growing demand for services from the sector. ValenciaportPCS currently offers more than 30 transactional and information services to over 1,100 companies and public bodies. It optimises and automates port and logistics processes through a single submission of data, while linking transport and logistics chains. The platform evolves continuously, whether to adapt its technology to legislative changes or to add new functionality.

articles.title: Democratic Sweep Puts Trump’s Maritime Agenda in Question
articles.summary: Democrats’ takeover of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections has raised new questions about the future of U.S. maritime policy, with implications for tariffs, shipbuilding, the Jones Act,...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network FILE PHOTO: U.S. President Donald Trump attends an event to sign executive orders in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., August 6, 2026. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein/File Photo Democrats’ takeover of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections has raised new questions about the future of U.S. maritime policy, with implications for tariffs, shipbuilding, the Jones Act, offshore energy, and the Trump administration’s military operations in the Middle East. The sweeping election results will leave President Donald Trump facing a Democratic-controlled Congress for the final two years of his presidency, giving lawmakers greater authority to challenge administration policies, conduct investigations, and determine federal spending priorities. For the maritime industry, the shift comes at a particularly consequential time. The administration is pursuing an ambitious plan to rebuild American shipbuilding and expand the U.S.-flag fleet, while its trade policies and ongoing war with Iran have disrupted global shipping markets. Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday directly blamed the Iran war for Republicans’ election losses. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote on X. The election raises questions about which maritime initiatives will retain bipartisan support, which could face increased scrutiny, and how much of the administration’s agenda can advance without congressional approval. Here are some of the major shipping issues now in play. The future of U.S. military operations against Iran is among the most immediate questions facing the incoming Congress, particularly after Vance’s acknowledgment of the war’s political consequences. The conflict has significantly disrupted commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, with repeated attacks on merchant vessels, restrictions on maritime traffic, and elevated tanker rates and war-risk insurance costs. The United States has maintained a naval blockade targeting Iranian maritime commerce, while Iran has continued to threaten and attack shipping in the region. Reuters reported Tuesday that Washington and Tehran remain far apart in negotiations to end the conflict. Iranian officials have demanded an end to the U.S. blockade, relief from oil sanctions, and the release of frozen funds as conditions for reopening Hormuz. With Democrats taking control of Congress, lawmakers could intensify scrutiny of the administration’s military strategy, the legal basis for continued operations, and the economic consequences of the conflict. Congress also controls defense appropriations and could consider measures aimed at limiting military operations or requiring additional authorization. Trump would retain substantial commander-in-chief authority, however, and any legislation restricting military operations could face a presidential veto. Trump’s tariff policies are another major area likely to come under pressure. The administration has imposed broad import duties on U.S. trading partners, creating uncertainty for international trade and influencing cargo volumes, sourcing decisions, and container shipping demand. Following a February Supreme Court ruling that invalidated tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, the administration turned to other trade authorities, including Sections 232 and 301, to maintain and expand its tariff program. Democrats have already indicated plans to challenge those policies. Senator Ron Wyden, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, has called for rolling back tariffs on Canadian goods and restoring a greater congressional role in trade policy. Congressional committees could investigate tariff exemptions, trade agreements, and the effects of import duties on U.S. businesses and consumers. For shipping, the implications extend to containerized imports, agricultural and industrial exports, and supply chains that have already adjusted to changing tariff deadlines. However, congressional control does not automatically eliminate existing tariffs. Trump retains veto authority, while federal trade laws provide the executive branch with considerable discretion to impose duties. The future of the administration’s Maritime Action Plan is another major question. Released in February, the plan outlines an ambitious effort to rebuild American commercial shipbuilding capacity, modernize shipyards, expand maritime workforce training, and increase the number of U.S.-flagged vessels operating in international commerce. Several major proposals require congressional legislation or funding, including new shipbuilding incentives, a Maritime Security Trust Fund, and financial assistance to support the construction and operation of American merchant ships. The administration has also proposed a universal fee on foreign-built commercial vessels calling at U.S. ports, assessed on the weight of imported cargo. According to the plan, a fee of one cent per kilogram could generate approximately $66 billion over ten years. Unlike existing measures targeting China-linked shipping, the proposal would apply to foreign-built vessels regardless of the country where they were constructed. How Congress approaches the proposed fee, its revenue, and the maritime programs it would finance remains an open question. At the same time, efforts to expand the U.S. maritime industrial base have attracted bipartisan interest, particularly amid growing concerns about China’s dominance in commercial shipbuilding. The SHIPS for America Act and related proposals to expand the U.S.-flag fleet could remain part of the legislative agenda, although their funding and implementation may face renewed debate. The change in congressional leadership also has implications for naval construction and military sealift. Congress determines annual defense authorizations and appropriations, including funding for warships, submarines, military support vessels, and shipyard modernization. Those decisions are increasingly important as commercial shipyards seek to expand into defense work, including Hanwha Philly Shipyard’s recent transition toward dual-use construction. Congress could examine Navy procurement priorities, shipbuilding delays, industrial capacity, and the balance between commercial and military vessel construction. The Maritime Administration’s Ready Reserve Force and other military sealift programs could also face additional scrutiny. The recent activation of the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel Empire State VII for an undisclosed military mission raises questions about the use of maritime training vessels for defense requirements, particularly when the administration is seeking to expand the number of qualified merchant mariners. Funding for the Maritime Security Program and Tanker Security Program, which provide access to privately operated U.S.-flag vessels for national defense purposes, will also remain subject to congressional decisions. The Jones Act is another area where increased congressional oversight could have direct consequences for domestic shipping. The law requires cargo transported between U.S. ports to move aboard qualifying U.S.-built, U.S.-owned, and U.S.-crewed vessels. Although the law enjoys longstanding bipartisan support, the administration’s use of emergency waivers during the Iran war has generated controversy among maritime unions and domestic vessel operators. The current waiver, which allows certain foreign-flagged vessels to transport energy products and other qualifying cargoes between U.S. ports, is scheduled to expire November 15. Nine maritime labor organizations recently raised concerns about the waiver’s compliance with federal law , including reporting requirements and restrictions on the use of foreign vessels. Their October 27 letter was addressed to Democratic members of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, including Ranking Member Rick Larsen and Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee Ranking Member Salud Carbajal. Both lawmakers could take on more influential oversight roles under the new congressional majority. The administration’s proposed fees targeting China-linked vessels are also facing an uncertain future, although they remain primarily under executive authority. The U.S. Trade Representative has proposed extending the current suspension of Section 301 maritime measures through January 9, 2027, while Washington and Beijing continue negotiations. The fees have faced opposition from shipping companies, ports, agricultural exporters, and manufacturers concerned about higher transportation costs. However, the issue cuts across party lines. Some Democratic lawmakers have supported aggressive trade measures targeting China’s maritime and shipbuilding industries, while others have questioned their potential economic consequences. Congress could revisit the fees as part of broader trade legislation or oversight, but USTR would retain significant authority over their implementation. Federal offshore energy policy is another area where the new Congress could influence maritime investment. The Trump administration has pursued policies restricting offshore wind development, including permitting delays and legal challenges affecting projects along the East Coast. Democratic lawmakers have generally supported offshore wind development, including the associated investment in ports, shipyards, and specialized vessels. Congress could use appropriations, legislation, and oversight hearings to challenge federal permitting decisions and support offshore wind infrastructure. The administration would nevertheless retain considerable authority over offshore leasing and permitting. Oil and gas policy could face similar congressional scrutiny, including federal offshore drilling programs, LNG export approvals, and environmental requirements. For shipping, these decisions could affect demand for LNG carriers, offshore support vessels, wind installation vessels, and other specialized marine assets. The election also raises questions about congressional oversight of sanctions enforcement, particularly measures targeting Russian oil exports and vessels involved in sanctions evasion. Congress enacted the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act in September, establishing additional sanctions and trade authorities. A Democratic-controlled Congress could examine how the administration is implementing those measures, including licensing decisions, exemptions, and enforcement against vessels involved in transporting sanctioned petroleum. The issue has taken on additional significance following recent controversy over potential Russian petroleum imports into the United States. For tanker operators, insurers, and commodity traders, changes in sanctions enforcement could have consequences for vessel employment, cargo flows, and compliance requirements. Federal funding for maritime infrastructure and the U.S. Coast Guard could also face changes under the new Congress. The Coast Guard is pursuing a major modernization effort, including fleet recapitalization, acquisition reforms, and new capabilities under its Force Design 2028 initiative. Congressional appropriations will influence funding for cutters, polar icebreakers, shore facilities, and maritime security operations. Meanwhile, federal port infrastructure and dredging programs remain dependent on congressional spending decisions. The Maritime Administration’s Port Infrastructure Development Program and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers navigation projects could face changes in funding priorities, environmental requirements, and project selection criteria. Lawmakers could also examine the administration’s efforts to streamline maritime infrastructure permitting, including recent changes to the federal review process for deepwater ports. The new congressional leadership could also revisit federal regulation of international ocean shipping. The Federal Maritime Commission oversees ocean carrier practices, including detention and demurrage charges, service contracts, and competition-related matters. Congress could revisit implementation of the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022 or consider additional measures addressing carrier practices and protections for American exporters. International shipping emissions policy is another potential area of oversight. The International Maritime Organization is scheduled to resume negotiations on its proposed Net-Zero Framework later this month, following the postponement of adoption last year. The Trump administration has opposed the framework’s proposed emissions-related financial mechanisms. Although the White House retains authority over the U.S. negotiating position at the IMO, Congress could examine the administration’s approach and consider domestic legislation or funding affecting maritime decarbonization, alternative fuels, and vessel emissions. articles.summary: The Iran war was a key driver of the Republican Party's shellacking in the US midterms on Tuesday, but the bruising defeat may make it more challenging for President Donald Trump to end the conflict.

REUTERS/Evan Vucci/File Photo By Ron Bousso LONDON, Nov 4 (Reuters) – The Iran war was a key driver of the Republican Party’s shellacking in the US midterms on Tuesday, but the bruising defeat may make it more challenging for President Donald Trump to end the conflict. Whether he opts for a new round of strikes, a quick deal with Iran or simply maintains the status quo, the president’s weakened position means the Middle East quagmire is likely to deepen. A sustainable solution for the region and global energy markets now looks even further away. Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday’s vote, scoring sweeping victories in several Republican strongholds for the first time in decades as voters delivered a stinging rebuke to Trump and his eight-month-old war in Iran. In the run-up to the vote, Trump sent conflicting messages about his next steps in the Middle East conflict. He refused to rule out a resumption of combat operations while also suggesting he was optimistic that a deal would be struck with Tehran to resolve a conflict that has severely disrupted oil and gas production in the world’s most important energy hub, sending global fuel prices soaring. The Democratic sweep ushers in a new period of divided government in Washington. Once the new Congress is seated next January, Trump will likely struggle to push through legislation and is apt to veto anything Congress sends his way. He may seek to operate via executive order, as he has throughout much of the past two years, but such actions are vulnerable to Supreme Court challenges. When it comes to foreign policy, however, Trump will continue to hold significant power. Although Congress could restrict funding for military operations in Iran, and technically should have declared war, the president retains broad authority to conduct military operations, especially once they are underway. The hostile political landscape in Washington is therefore unlikely to force the president’s hand. Trump may ultimately pursue the option most likely to lower energy prices, but don’t expect that to deliver lasting peace. STALEMATE The Iran war, launched by Israel and the US on February 28, initially had multiple aims, including destroying Tehran’s military capabilities and preventing it from developing a nuclear weapon, with government change also encouraged. But since June the conflict has largely morphed into a battle over control of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway that previously transported a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas. While energy flows collapsed to near zero in the first months of the war, crude oil shipments through the strait have recovered to around 80% of pre-war levels in recent months, thanks to US Navy-assisted tanker convoys. But oil prices remain around 40% above pre-war levels, reflecting the elevated risk of transporting oil out of the region. At the same time, the US has imposed an effective blockade on Iran’s oil exports, squeezing the country’s vital source of revenue. Both Washington and Tehran therefore had reasons to seek a diplomatic resolution before the midterms, and the Republican thrashing seemingly gave the administration more incentive. Yet the result has mostly highlighted how bad all of the president’s options are. NO WAY OUT? The US administration seemingly has three options: further strikes, a quick deal or the status quo. On Monday, the second option appeared possible. In recent weeks, Qatar has been mediating indirect talks between Washington and Tehran. News that Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had given the negotiators more leeway to make a deal helped send Brent crude prices LCOc1tumbling more than 14% since Monday. Yet Iran later squelched this optimism, saying the sides remain far apart. At the heart of the negotiations are Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Trump has consistently held that Tehran must never obtain a nuclear bomb, though he has sent mixed signals over whether he would accept a civilian nuclear program. Iranian officials in recent weeks have argued that any talks about its nuclear ambitions should be held at a later stage and that negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, releasing Iranian funds held overseas and easing sanctions on Tehran. Now that Trump has been weakened politically, Tehran will have little reason to quickly agree to a deal that is not in its favor. Yet if he signs a deal that fails to meaningfully restrict Iran’s nuclear program, Trump would essentially be admitting defeat, something he may be especially loath to do. While an agreement that fully reopens Hormuz could lower oil prices in the short term, a quick deal that doesn’t resolve or even address the core issues would leave the Middle East in a precarious position in which Iran would likely hold significantly more power than it did before the war began. This risks further undermining US relations with its Gulf allies and laying the foundations for a new confrontation. Trump’s option of further strikes is underpinned by a significant US military buildup in the Middle East. Two aircraft carrier strike groups are already in or near the region, with a third heading toward the Gulf, according to US media reports. Together, they would constitute one of the largest US military deployments to the region in decades. Deploying so much military muscle is not cheap, so this appears to indicate Trump’s intentions. Yet the administration faces a familiar problem. A limited military campaign likely has little chance of fundamentally weakening Iran’s rulers, while a broader campaign risks dragging the US deeper into a deeply unpopular war. The electorate’s strong opposition to the conflict makes a brief campaign far more likely than a major operation, but it risks resulting in more casualties, more damage to energy infrastructure and little change in either side’s negotiating positions. SHAKY STATUS QUO Finally, Trump could opt to maintain the status quo, hoping that the US blockade on Iran will eventually lead to the collapse of the government, or at least force it to concede ground in peace talks. That may happen eventually, but time isn’t on Trump’s side. As we enter the final two years of the Trump era, the president will likely be keen to ensure his legacy is not defined by a military quagmire. The problem for him is that there is no obvious off-ramp. The biggest loser is the Middle East. Whether it faces a new round of military strikes, a flimsy peace deal that emboldens Iran or a tense status quo, the region and global energy markets are likely to enter a highly unstable era. Tuesday’s vote may have weakened Trump’s desire to remain in the Middle East, but it did not bring the region any closer to peace. articles.title: Neptune Pacific supports Tuvalu’s first commercial export in 24 years
articles.summary: Neptune Pacific has transported Tuvalu’s first commercial export since 2002, helping a local skincare producer reach the New Zealand market. articles.body: Neptune Pacific has transported Tuvalu’s first commercial export since 2002, helping a local skincare producer reach the New Zealand market. The shipment comprised 2,102 units of Fenua Ola skincare products made from extra-virgin coconut oil. It departed Funafuti for Auckland in June 2026. Neptune Pacific provided the freight service free of charge to mark the milestone. The carrier also helped the six-person Fenua Ola team prepare the cargo and complete the necessary export documentation. A formal handover ceremony took place in Tuvalu on 27 June. Coconut industry creates new export opportunity Fenua Ola was developed through efforts to revive Tuvalu’s coconut industry. The initiative forms part of the Tuvalu Coconut Rehabilitation Programme, led by the Government of Tuvalu with financial support from the European Union. The programme aims to restore coconut production and create higher-value products from local resources. A UK-based development consultancy also provided technical assistance during the development of the skincare range. “Given Tuvalu’s remote location and shipping complexities, this collaboration played a significant role in Fenua Ola’s success and sets a strong foundation for future Tuvalu exports,” said Andrew Jacque, Agricultural Policy Advisor. Tuvalu is one of the world’s smallest and most remote island nations. Its geography limits large-scale production and makes the country heavily dependent on imported goods. Neptune Pacific has served Tuvalu for more than 20 years. At times, it has been the only shipping line providing regular cargo connections for the country’s population of around 10,000 people. “The successful launch of Fenua Ola’s first shipment is a testament to the progress achieved through vision, perseverance and partnership,” said Lauti Bici, Chief Executive Officer of manufacturer Tama Tuvalu. Jason Ward, Owner’s Representative for Neptune Pacific, said shipping services in remote South Pacific markets play an important role in helping local businesses reach overseas customers. “Operating shipping services in remote parts of the South Pacific is about more than moving cargo. It’s also about helping local businesses access new markets and opportunities,” he stated.

articles.title: SubSea Craft, NSI Demonstrate Autonomous Systems in Maritime Exercise
articles.summary: U.S.-based Naval Systems, Inc. (in partnership with Dragonfish Technical Solutions, LLC) (NSI/DF) and U.K.-based SubSea Craft successfully demonstrated an integrated suite of advanced unmanned maritime systems during a multinational maritime…
articles.body: SubSea Craft, NSI Demonstrate Autonomous Systems in Maritime Exercise Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 4, 2026 © SubSea Craft © SubSea Craft U.S.-based Naval Systems, Inc. (in partnership with Dragonfish Technical Solutions, LLC) (NSI/DF) and U.K.-based SubSea Craft successfully demonstrated an integrated suite of advanced unmanned maritime systems during a multinational maritime exercise conducted October 5–8 off the coast of California. At the request of the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research & Engineering (OUSW(R&E)) exercise personnel, SubSea Craft and NSI/DF combined their autonomous systems to deliver an integrated demonstration capability, pairing SubSea Craft's MARS Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) with NSI/DF's Arowana Unmanned Undersea Vehicle (UUV). Following initial planning and design, the systems were integrated, tested and successfully demonstrated within 48 hours, highlighting how new capabilities can be rapidly fielded in response to evolving operational requirements. During the exercise, the integrated MARS-Arowana capability demonstrated over-the-horizon engagements against surface targets in the open ocean. Multiple NSI/DF Arowana UUVs were launched from SubSea Craft's MARS USV to conduct simulated kinetic engagements, with repeated successful runs demonstrating the accuracy, endurance and operational potential of the combined system. In a second demonstration, SubSea Craft and NSI/DF showcased an underwater launch capability integrating the NSI Arowana UUV with SubSea Craft's CADDIS Unmanned Aerial System (UAS), a diver-deployable platform. The concept enables divers to deploy both systems from underwater. The CADDIS UAS travels to the surface before transitioning to flight and proceeding towards a designated target, with information relayed to the Arowana UUV. Independently deployed from underwater by divers, the Arowana can then proceed towards the designated surface target. All three technologies were selected to participate during Maritime Big Play Pacific through the U.S. Navy BARB solicitation, which sought promising solutions for the emerging undersea warfare battlespace. The BARB assessments took place as part of the larger OUSW(R&E)-sponsored event.

articles.title: Port of Gothenburg reports stable freight flows
articles.summary: Cargo volumes at the Port of Gothenburg developed steadily from January to September 2026. articles.body: Cargo volumes at the Port of Gothenburg developed steadily from January to September 2026. Container volumes were in line with the previous year, while several segments grew clearly: new cars rose 14% and energy products 10%, and Ro/Ro traffic and rail volumes also continued to increase. The port handled 698,000 TEU in the period, against 699,000 TEU a year earlier. Behind the largely unchanged total lies a 2% rise in laden containers and an 11% fall in empty container handling, meaning more cargo and less air than before. Imports of laden containers increased 7%, while exports decreased 1%. Around 60 percent of containers are moved by rail to or from the hinterland. Rail volumes reached 403,000 TEU, up 2 percent on the same period last year, which puts rail traffic on course for another record year. Claes Sundmark, Vice President Sales & Marketing at the Port of Gothenburg, said development is stable across all cargo segments in a market that remains hard to assess, and that growing volumes in every segment show the port remains a strong and reliable freight hub for Swedish foreign trade. He described the port’s rail system, Railport Scandinavia, as crucial to its offering, strengthening the competitiveness of Swedish industry by connecting import and export regions across the country with the port’s maritime services in an efficient and sustainable way.

articles.title: Maersk changes PCD logic for European import shipments
articles.summary: Maersk will change how it calculates inland charges for selected import shipments across 15 European countries. The new Price Calculation Date (PCD) logic will apply to import shipments created from 1 January 2027. The change covers Bills of Lading booked with a CY move where customers add destination last-mile...
articles.body: Maersk will change how it calculates inland charges for selected import shipments across 15 European countries. The new Price Calculation Date (PCD) logic will apply to import shipments created from 1 January 2027. The change covers Bills of Lading booked with a CY move where customers add destination last-mile delivery later through an import shipment. Under the current system, Maersk calculates inland charges using the Ocean Booking PCD. This includes fuel-related charges. From January, the carrier will instead use the date on which the import shipment is created. Maersk said the change aims to reduce pricing mismatches and delays when applying inland charges and fuel adjustments. The revised process will apply in: Albania Bosnia and Herzegovina Croatia Cyprus Czech Republic Greece Hungary Italy North Macedonia Malta Montenegro San Marino Serbia Slovakia Slovenia Store Door bookings remain unchanged The change will not affect Bills of Lading booked with a Store Door move at destination. For these shipments, Maersk will continue calculating inland charges according to the Ocean Booking PCD. For non-FMC, non-SPOT bookings, the Ocean Booking PCD is the scheduled departure date of the first sea leg at the time of booking confirmation. For FMC-regulated non-SPOT bookings, the PCD is the final container gate-in date. articles.title: Freightos Weekly Update: Asia – US air rates already nearing last year’s high on peak season volumes
articles.summary: Even with more container vessels routing back through the Red Sea on Asia – Europe services, and estimations of slumping post-peak demand, carriers have been able to push rates up 10% to N. Europe and 23% to the Mediterranean over the past month. Prices ticked up 3% last week to $4,375/FEU to the Mediterranean and […]
articles.body: Even with more container vessels routing back through the Red Sea on Asia – Europe services, and estimations of slumping post-peak demand, carriers have been able to push rates up 10% to N. Europe and 23% to the Mediterranean over the past month. Prices ticked up 3% last week to $4,375/FEU to the Mediterranean and were about level at $3,595/FEU to N. Europe. Congestion in N. Europe hubs, as well as some lingering backlogs in the Far East may be helping put some degree of upward pressure on rates, with a recent one-day port worker union strike across many ports in Europe as well as other regions, possibly adding to backlogs. Carriers planned GRIs of $1,000 – $1,500/FEU for these lanes to start the month and additional increases for mid-November. Daily rates so far this week have stayed flat, but the coming days will indicate if carriers go through with the price hikes and if they’ll succeed, with some forwarders skeptical that market conditions will support further increases. Even with transpacific rates still at peak levels, carriers have GRIs of $2,000 – $3,000/FEU set to start the month for these lanes as well, though here too rates so far this week have not climbed and some forwarders think more increases are unlikely as this trade finally enters slow season. East Coast rates cooled 6% compared to last week’s bump, but are still $200/FEU higher than two weeks ago at about $9,900/FEU, with West Coast prices about level since climbing to the $8,300/FEU range in September. Asia – Europe rates are climbing relative to September, but from July to September prices fell $2,000 – $3,000/FEU on these lanes, about back to their pre-peak season baseline in mid-May. Meanwhile, the surprising rate resilience on the transpacific – including post-Golden Week, with prices currently about $5,500/FEU higher than before peak season – and the relatively short amount of time left until demand is likely to pick up ahead of Lunar New Year may make it unlikely that transpacific prices will fall back anywhere close to their pre-peak baseline before they climb again. Another factor that could help prop rates up even as demand cools is the potential port worker union strike at LA/Long Beach. The Local 26 watchmen union, part of the ILWU, has been working under an expired contract since mid-2025 and last week voted to authorize a strike as early as November 1st. Over the weekend though, the union agreed to extend the current contract until 5pm PT on November 4th to allow additional time for negotiations, with federal mediators now involved. A strike by the relatively small union could have an outsized impact on port operations as these workers provide required security services at many of the terminals. In air cargo, Far East – N. America rates continued to climb last week, increasing 9% to $7.76/kg from the peak season demand bump. This price level – a high for the year – is up 40% compared to this time last year, and is approaching the 2025 peak of $8.00/kg reached early last December. Asia – Europe rates were about level at $4.39/kg last week and are 11% higher year on year, but are well short of highs of about $5.25/kg seen earlier this year, as the market continues to adjust to decreases in e-commerce volumes on this lane. Judah Levine, Head of Research, Freightos Group (Nasdaq: CRGO)

From July 1, 2029, the prohibition will extend to all scrubber systems, including closed-loop installations. The measure follows a proposal by parliamentarian Justus Hansen of the Demokraatit party. The government had proposed the phased timetable in line with an emerging regional approach under the OSPAR Convention, which covers the Northeast Atlantic. Scrubbers, formally known as exhaust gas cleaning systems (EGCS), allow ships to continue burning higher-sulfur fuel by washing sulfur oxides from exhaust gases. Open-loop systems use seawater and discharge the resulting wastewater directly overboard, carrying sulfur compounds, heavy metals and other contaminants into the marine environment. Closed-loop systems recirculate the washwater but can also generate waste streams requiring disposal. The Clean Arctic Alliance welcomed the decision. Its lead adviser, Sian Prior, said: “Scrubbers simply offer a loophole for ships to continue burning the most polluting fuels – instead of using widely available cleaner fuels such as marine gas oil.” The alliance argues that scrubbers shift pollution from the atmosphere into the ocean while allowing ships to continue burning residual fuels that generate higher levels of particulate matter and black carbon than cleaner distillate fuels. The decision comes amid a broader tightening of shipping regulations across the Arctic, although the different measures address distinct pollution problems. On March 1, 2026, the Canadian Arctic and the Norwegian Sea became IMO-designated Emission Control Areas (ECAs) . The designations require ships to meet stricter nitrogen oxide and sulfur oxide emission standards, including a maximum sulfur content of 0.10% in marine fuel. Norway already had an ECA covering its North Sea waters. Svalbard has gone further on fuel quality. Since January 2022, ships entering its territorial waters have been prohibited from using or carrying petroleum-based fuels with properties exceeding those permitted for marine gas oil. The wider Arctic, however, still lacks a comprehensive ECA covering the entire region. Nor do existing ECAs eliminate the use of heavy fuel oil in every circumstance: scrubber-equipped vessels can generally meet sulfur limits while continuing to burn residual fuels. The IMO’s separate Arctic heavy fuel oil prohibition , adopted under MARPOL Annex I, began taking effect in July 2024 for some vessels. Certain ships meeting specified fuel-tank protection standards have until July 1, 2029, to comply. The prohibition addresses the risk and consequences of HFO spills rather than scrubber wastewater or black carbon emissions. The impact on Greenland’s cruise industry remains unclear, as there is no publicly available breakdown of how many vessels calling in Greenlandic waters are equipped with scrubbers. Greenland and its surrounding waters received approximately 94,000 cruise passengers across 232 voyages in 2025, according to the Arctic Council. For comparison, global fleet data compiled by S&P Global in 2025 identified 338 passenger and cruise ships equipped with scrubbers. Vessels affected by the new restrictions would not necessarily have to abandon Greenlandic itineraries or remove their equipment, however. Operators could instead switch to compliant, lower-sulfur fuels such as marine gas oil (MGO), avoiding the need to discharge scrubber wastewater. articles.title: Switch Maritime, Incat Crowther Secure US Agreement for Hydrogen Ferry
articles.summary: Switch Maritime and Incat Crowther have secured a Design Basis Agreement (DBA) with the United States Coast Guard (USCG) for their SWITCH-150 hydrogen fuel cell-electric fast ferry, marking a regulatory milestone in the development of the 150…
articles.body: Switch Maritime, Incat Crowther Secure US Agreement for Hydrogen Ferry Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 4, 2026 (Credit: Incat Crowther) Switch Maritime and Incat Crowther have secured a Design Basis Agreement (DBA) with the United States Coast Guard (USCG) for their SWITCH-150 hydrogen fuel cell-electric fast ferry, marking a regulatory milestone in the development of the 150-passenger vessel. The agreement establishes a regulatory framework to guide the vessel's construction, commissioning and eventual operation, with the design intended to deliver performance comparable to diesel-powered ferries while producing only water vapour as vessel emissions. The SWITCH-150 combines hydrogen fuel cell-electric propulsion with onboard hydrogen storage, allowing it to operate on high-frequency ferry routes without requiring shoreside charging infrastructure or changes to service schedules to accommodate charging. The vessel is designed to be refuelled using mobile hydrogen equipment, with a daily bunkering schedule. The 28.5-meter aluminium ferry will have a 9-metre beam and accommodation for 150 passengers and six crew members. Its propulsion system comprises six 225 kW fuel cells, four 588 kW electric motors driving four propellers and a 1,576 kWh battery system, supported by four compressed hydrogen tanks with a combined capacity of 720 kilograms. The vessel is designed for a service speed of 25 knots and a maximum speed of 27.5 knots. The hydrogen storage capacity is intended to provide sufficient range for a full day of operations across various New York ferry routes. The passenger deck will include seating for 150 people, luggage storage, a kiosk, three bathrooms, including a wheelchair-accessible facility, and large windows. The first SWITCH-150 is intended to operate in New York City, based at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, with the project supported by a $2 million grant from the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA). “Signing the DBA with the Coast Guard is a critical milestone in advancing the development of the SWITCH-150. With the DBA in hand, Switch, our project team, and the USCG have a clear and defined framework that will inform vessel construction, commissioning, and ultimately operation,” said Francisco Planells, Director of the Newbuild Program, Switch Maritime. The new design builds on the regulatory and operating framework established by Sea Change, the first hydrogen fuel cell-electric ferry in the United States, also designed by Incat Crowther. Sea Change received its USCG Design Basis Agreement in 2020 and its Certificate of Inspection in 2024, allowing it to begin passenger service in July of that year. For the SWITCH-150, the project team worked with the USCG to establish a framework demonstrating equivalent safety and risk mitigation measures for hydrogen propulsion and storage. The International Maritime Organization's Interim Guidelines for the Safety of Ships Using Hydrogen as Fuel, approved in May 2026, also provided a foundation for the agreement. With the DBA secured, Incat Crowther will move forward with detailed design development and preparation of a digital shipbuilding package for construction.

The deal brings MPC Oceanic closer to one of the world’s largest crew management providers, with more than 16,000 seafarers serving onboard vessels at any given time and crewing services covering over 1,150 ships worldwide. Marlow also employs more than 1,300 shore-based staff across 13 countries. For Marlow, the investment forms part of a generational transition at the company founded by Hermann Eden, who remains chairman, while opening up access to MPC Oceanic’s investment capacity, technology and wider maritime services network. MPC Oceanic chief executive Constantin Baack said the partnership would strengthen the group’s position in crew management and training, particularly as more complex propulsion systems, alternative fuels and tightening regulations place greater demands on seafarers. The move adds another major shipmanagement business to MPC Oceanic’s portfolio, which already includes Wilhelmsen Ahrenkiel Ship Management. In December 2023, the group, then operating as MPC Capital, joined forces with Wilhelmsen Ship Management to acquire Hamburg-based Zeaborn Ship Management, which had around 100 vessels under management at the time. MPC adopted its current name in September this year, reflecting its expansion beyond investment management into ship operations, maritime services and energy infrastructure. The group currently manages and operates more than 400 vessels and energy assets. For Marlow, the deal marks a fresh ownership development four years after it abandoned plans to merge with fellow Cyprus-based Columbia Shipmanagement. The two companies had explored a combination since 2017 but called off the proposed merger in October 2022, having continued to operate independently throughout. articles.title: TotalEnergies forges pacts with Petronas, Sonangol, and Oil India to slash methane footprint
articles.summary: TotalEnergies has deepened partnerships across Malaysia, Angola, and India to expand advanced methane detection and accelerate emissions cuts.
articles.body: Energy Transition November 4, 2026 · 2 hours ago TotalEnergies forges pacts with Petronas, Sonangol, and Oil India to slash methane footprint TotalEnergies has deepened partnerships across Malaysia, Angola, and India to expand advanced methane detection and accelerate emissions cuts. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: TotalEnergies As global pressure mounts to curb greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, France’s energy giant TotalEnergies has revealed a trio of new partnerships across geographies, joining forces with national oil companies (NOCs) in Malaysia, Angola, and India to share its cutting-edge methane-tracking technology and drive toward a near-zero emissions future by 2030. During the meeting of the Oil and Gas Decarbonization Charter (OGDC) member companies in Abu Dhabi, TotalEnergies has highlighted its cooperation with national oil and gas companies to reduce methane emissions through its partnerships with Petronas in Malaysia, Sonangol in Angola, and Oil India Limited (OIL) in India. To this end, the French firm has signed a collaboration agreement with Petronas, the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC) , and JGC Corporation to contribute to the development of the Southeast Asia Methane Emissions Technology Evaluation Center (SEA METEC), which will be a regional center based in Malaysia and dedicated to evaluating methane emissions measurement and monitoring technologies across Southeast Asia. Related Articles Fossil Energy COP28 brings ‘historic’ action as 50 oil & gas players pen decarbonization charter 7 min read The European giant will support the development of SEA METEC by sharing the expertise gained over more than ten years through its own TotalEnergies Anomalies Detection Initiative (TADI) center, Europe’s only facility dedicated to evaluating methane detection and quantification technologies. SEA METEC is expected to strengthen knowledge sharing and support the harmonization of methane emissions measurement and quantification methodologies, enabling companies to better detect, measure, and ultimately curtail their emissions. Patrick Pouyanné , Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of TotalEnergies, commented: “Our cooperation with Petronas in Malaysia, Sonangol in Angola and OIL in India illustrates TotalEnergies’ commitment to the OGDC and the momentum it has created among international and national companies. “I am convinced that by sharing technologies, expertise and best practices, we can accelerate concrete action and contribute to our common ambition of achieving near-zero upstream methane emissions by 2030.” Related Articles Fossil Energy TotalEnergies ups methane detection ante and signs up another firm to its drone-based tech 5 min read TotalEnergies has also inked a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Sonangol to strengthen technical cooperation on methane emissions reduction and decarbonization solutions in Angola. The agreement builds on the experience gained through the AUSEA technology and covers methane emissions detection, measurement, monitoring, and reduction, as well as the sharing of best practices, methodologies, and technical expertise. The two companies are working together to identify concrete solutions to reduce methane emissions and flaring, improve energy efficiency, support facility electrification, and advance carbon management solutions. The cooperation is also covering greenhouse gas emissions reporting, technical training, and knowledge sharing, as well as the exploration of financing opportunities, including potential support from the World Bank’s Global Flaring and Methane Reduction (GFMR) Fund. Related Articles Business & Finance TotalEnergies earmarks annual spend of up to $17 billion over next five years 3 min read Building on a first campaign using TotalEnergies’ AUSEA technology to detect and quantify methane emissions over 20 OIL-operated sites in Assam, Oil India and TotalEnergies are strengthening their collaboration with a second field campaign. The first one-month-long campaign provided OIL with data to support its emissions reporting, while demonstrating AUSEA’s ability to accurately detect and quantify methane emissions across diverse sites and field conditions. A second month-long campaign will extend the use of AUSEA to additional OIL-operated sites, further strengthening the cooperation between the two companies on methane emissions reduction. articles.body: Contracts & Tenders November 4, 2026 · 1 minute ago Fugro wins East Anglia Two post-installation survey contract AB Adrijana Buljan Offshore Wind 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email An offshore wind farm in the North Sea; Source: Fugro Fugro has secured a contract from Cadeler to carry out post-installation seabed surveys at the 960 MW East Anglia Two offshore wind farm in the UK, with work scheduled to begin in early 2027. The company will deploy its FCV 600 work-class remotely operated vehicle (ROV) from a Cadeler installation vessel to inspect 64 monopile foundation locations. The surveys will verify that the foundations have been installed as planned and provide data to support quality assurance and assessment of their long-term integrity. Cadeler is responsible for transporting and installing all 64 monopile foundations and wind turbines at East Anglia Two. The company will use its newbuild A-class vessel Wind Ace alongside an O-class vessel for the installation campaign. East Anglia Two is being developed by ScottishPower Renewables, part of the Iberdrola Group, approximately 33 kilometres off the Suffolk coast. The 960 MW project will comprise 64 Siemens Gamesa SG 14-236 DD turbines and is expected to enter commercial operation in late 2028. Fugro is also providing positioning and construction services to Cadeler at Ørsted’s 2.9 GW Hornsea 3 offshore wind farm, where its specialists aboard Cadeler’s Wind Ally installation vessel are using the company’s InclinoCam technology to measure the tilt and vertical alignment of monopile foundations during installation, according to the company. articles.title: Sea1's first methanol-ready offshore energy support vessel fitted with offshore crane and helideck
articles.summary: Sea1 Offshore's first of four 120-meter-long offshore energy support vessels (OESVs) being built in China has been fitted with an offshore crane...
articles.body: Vessels & Vehicles November 4, 2026 · 1 minute ago Sea1's first methanol-ready offshore energy support vessel fitted with offshore crane and helideck NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Sea1 Diamond. Source: Sea1 Offshore Sea1 Offshore's first of four 120-meter-long offshore energy support vessels (OESVs) being built in China has been fitted with an offshore crane and helicopter deck, with delivery expected in January. Norwegian offshore services provider Sea1 Offshore placed the order for the first two OESVs with Cosco Shipping in November 2024, revealing at the time that negotiations were ongoing for the delivery of more vessels. The contract for the construction of two additional vessels was announced in March 2025. The construction of the first vessel, named Sea1 Diamond, began in September 2025, with the second, named Sea1 Citrine, following in December . Sea1 Diamond, launched at the yard in July , is currently undergoing outfitting and commissioning at the COSCO Nantong Shipyard, with the offshore crane and helicopter deck installed, as Sea1 Offshore reported on November 3. According to the Norwegian firm, the 250 T Huisman crane is designed for subsea lifting operations down to 3,000 meters, while the helicopter deck is dimensioned for Sikorsky S-92. The vessel is expected to be delivered in January 2027. Sea1 Offshore also reported that the OESV is still uncommitted and open for clients after delivery. Based on the ST-245 design, the OESVs will have a cargo deck of 1,400 square meters, and each will be equipped with a 250-ton deck crane, two remotely operated vehicle (ROV) hangars, and a moonpool. They will provide accommodation for up to 120 personnel. The vessels will be methanol-ready, with generators that can operate on 100% biofuel, and will be capable of serving both the oil & gas sector and the renewable energy market.
